# MQ-C04-014 — Finitude of dimensions, infinite space, and geometrical demonstrations

**Arabic source:** source characters 780567–789608, printed markers I.320–324. **Status:** explanatory first-pass rendering, source ordering retained; proof diagrams and damaged electronic readings require checking against print.

### All bodily dimensions are finite

Another property of bodies is that their **dimensions terminate** (*mutanāhiyat al-abʿād*). It is counted among propositions about bodies because corporeal extension unquestionably exists, whereas the existence of void is disputed. A doctrine allowing dimensions without limit is reported from Indian sages, various ancient philosophers, and the later philosopher Abū al-Barakāt. The famous arguments against it number three.

**First, the demonstration from alignment (*burhān al-musāmata*).** Imagine a rotating sphere and a line moving with it, originally parallel to another straight line. As the sphere turns, the moving line passes from being parallel—that is, never meeting the other line however far both are extended—to **aligning with** it, which means the extended lines meet. Since the alignment begins after an absence of alignment, it must have a first point of alignment. But if the line extends infinitely, no first point can be assigned: at every alleged point of alignment the motion and the angle can be divided further, yielding a still earlier alignment. The construction speaks of an imagined point, for a line need not contain an actual separate point until it is really divided. The rotation makes the transition from parallelism to meeting particularly evident, almost sensible.

**Objection:** If motion and angle are divisible without end, the argument itself has shown there cannot be a first point; it has not established that an infinite dimension is impossible. **Reply:** that is precisely the reductio: upon supposing infinite extension, the construction requires both the beginning of alignment and its absence. One cannot answer a valid conditional proof merely by asserting the negation of its consequent while retaining the antecedent. The impossibility lies in the combined supposition. More directly: with the infinite dimension and the stated construction, either alignment has a first point or it does not; each option leads to the stated difficulty.

**Further objection:** the beginning of alignment might be a **beginning in time** without being a first **point along the line**. **Reply:** the time of the event corresponds to the movement, and the movement to positions along the distance; absence of the first position would imply absence of the first stage of movement and of the first interval. **Further objection:** the contradiction may result from the whole construction rather than infinite extension alone. **Reply:** the other parts of the construction are independently possible, so the incompatible element must be the assumption of limitless extension. **Further objection:** imagined subdivisions of motion and angle have no authority over an infinite external line. **Reply:** judgments of geometrical imagination follow reason sufficiently closely to function as near-sensible demonstrations; it is mere *wahm* falsely applied beyond its field—such as requiring every existent to have spatial position—that gives deceptive judgments.

Al-Rāzī reverses the argument: if a point is aligned in sequence with points higher up an indefinitely extended line, the same construction appears to establish **infinitely many** points above the endpoint of the world's axis. The reported example supposes a rotating diameter parallel to that axis and the possibility of drawing the line that bisects the angle arising as the diameter turns. The reply is that no independently given infinite region beyond the world has been established. Merely drawing geometrical lines in thought does not prove an externally existing void or plenum outside the cosmic limit. The author's response to al-Rāzī's appeal to an allegedly necessary judgment of intellect is exceptionally dismissive: the claimed necessity is itself disputed.

**Second, the ladder or wedge demonstration (*al-burhān al-sullamī*).** Its aim is to show that, if dimensions had no end, an infinite magnitude would be contained **between two limiting lines**, an impossibility. Draw two rays from one vertex at an angle. The farther they are extended, the greater the distance between them. If they go on without limit, that distance increases without end. Ibn Sīnā objected to the older version that *always increasing* does not entail the existence of an **actually infinite** distance: at every finite stage one can obtain a greater distance, without any single transverse line being infinite. The proof therefore needs further argument.

The revised proof chooses a base segment connecting corresponding points of the two rays and treats further extension of both sides proportionally. The increase in each new transverse distance has the same ratio to the original transverse distance as the increase in the rays has to their original length. Suppose the successive increases equal: if the rays were infinite, the transverse line would be the sum of infinitely many equal positive increments; it would then be an actually infinite magnitude. Insisting that an increasing line always consists only of finite stages is not enough if one has granted a complete infinitely long side. The case of indefinitely *decreasing* subdivisions must be distinguished, since a finite magnitude can be divided into progressively smaller portions without becoming infinite in length. The most direct version, attributed to the Illuminationist, arranges the angle so that the transverse segment is **equal to each side**. A finite segment cannot equal an infinite side.

To make that arrangement explicit, choose a triangle whose angles are all two-thirds of a right angle: the three angles are equal and, by Euclid, so are the three sides. The distance joining corresponding points on the extending rays is therefore equal to the corresponding lengths of the rays. Suhrawardī's **shield demonstration** (*al-burhān al-tursī*) begins instead with a circular object divided from its centre by six equal rays, each subtending an angle of two-thirds of a right angle. Each sector gives an equilateral triangle when a transverse line joins the sides. An indefinitely extended pair of rays would force an indefinitely extended base contained between them. Someone who denies this equality without challenging the Euclidean proposition does not, on the author's view, appreciate the geometry.

**Objections and replies.** The construction may prove only that transverse distances grow without any fixed upper bound, not that one existent transverse interval is infinite. To posit a *last* connecting line would already suppose the rays terminate, begging the question. The reply insists that the hypothesized complete infinite sides are **equal in magnitude** to their base in this very figure: if the base is bounded between its endpoints, it is finite, and the supposedly infinite equal sides must be finite too. This is a reductio, not an inference that the base first acquires a final endpoint by assuming finite sides. One may also suggest that the absurdity arises from the whole configuration. As before, the other specified conditions are judged independently possible, so the burden lies on the claim that the unlimited rays can coexist with them.

**Third, the correspondence demonstration (*burhān al-taṭbīq*).** Suppose an infinite extension, remove a cubit from one end, and align the diminished extension with the entire original. Either every cubit of the greater has a corresponding cubit in the lesser, in which case the whole and its proper part are equal, or there is an unmatched cubit, in which case the shorter extension ends and the greater, exceeding it by one cubit, must also end. The objections to this proof were already given in the earlier discussion of infinite regress and need not be repeated here. They include whether imaginative alignment is permissible, whether pairing establishes equality of magnitudes, and whether the argument applies only to ordered positional magnitudes rather than to abstract number or the succession of celestial revolutions.

### Qualifications of the three proofs

The **alignment proof** assumes rejection of an indivisible spatial substance: the motion and angle must be divisible indefinitely for its characteristic paradox to arise. The **ladder proof** assumes that the proposed infinitude extends in the directions needed to let the rays spread indefinitely; the shield formulation especially assumes unlimited extension in all relevant directions. It can thus serve as a reductio against someone allowing infinite extension in **all** directions without necessarily refuting every proposal of infinitude in only one direction. The **correspondence proof** depends on assumptions about applying imagined one-to-one correspondence to actual size and on the weak inference from correspondence to equality.

The numerous other demonstrations of the finitude of bodily dimensions chiefly modify these three or borrow from proofs against an infinite regress. One variation of the alignment proof, termed the **proof from passing beyond**, imagines a ray extending without limit from the centre of a sphere and asks whether an advancing body can pass beyond what is designated as one of its directional parts. If it cannot, this part alone is the direction; if it can, the motion must be **away from** the first direction or **toward** the second. An objection that it simply moves *within* the direction is answered that motion within something divisible must still bear toward or away from one of its limits. Thus a **direction taken as an endpoint of motion or reference** cannot itself be a further occupied extended distance. This is enough to reject bodily occupation of an alleged unlimited direction, without proving that every direction is literally a dimensionless point: a limit may in some respects be a line or surface.

A final distinction matters. Is a direction the extremity of **each particular body's** extension, or must it terminate **all** possible extensions and every line of indication? A body's own surface ends its extension without thereby defining an absolute cosmic direction. The latter interpretation, identifying the ultimate boundaries of direction with the outermost limiting surface, is preferred. The discussion of the familiar six directions accordingly requires a further investigation.

*Editorial note:* The philosophical soundness of these medieval reductio arguments is a separate question from faithfully representing them. The text itself records substantial challenges, especially the difference between indefinite divisibility and an actually completed infinite magnitude.

# MQ-C04-015 — Directions and the temporal origination of bodies

**Arabic source:** source characters 789608–799973, printed markers I.324–330. **Status:** source-ordered explanatory first pass; not print-collated or clause-verified.

### Are there precisely six directions?

**Directions** (*jihāt*) are not intrinsically restricted to any number: one can imagine indefinitely numerous rays issuing from one point of a body. Six are commonly distinguished for two reasons. First, a body admits three intersecting dimensions and each dimension has two ends, making six extremities. Second, ordinary speech takes the human body as its measure: head and feet give above and below, face and back give before and behind, and the two flanks—associated with the generally stronger right hand and weaker left—give right and left. These are transferred by likeness to other animals: for quadrupeds, for example, the back and belly correspond to above and below, and head and tail to before and behind. Neither convention establishes that there can **only** be six directions.

Of these directions, the philosophers distinguish **up and down as natural**; the remaining four are **positional**. The latter change as a person turns: when he faces east, east is before him and west behind him, but on turning west the labels reverse, as do right and left relative to north and south. Above and below, however, do not exchange their places simply because a person stands on his head. What faces his head then lies below, and what faces his feet above, but the directions themselves remain. Likewise people standing on opposite ends of a terrestrial diameter each have the head above and feet below.

An objection takes above and below to be **correlatives** and concludes that neither can be conceived or exist without the other, just as front/back and right/left seem paired. The answer distinguishes **above from the thing which has an above**: these are genuinely correlatives. It does not follow that the directions above and below depend on one another in precisely this way. One can conceive one direction without the other; an illustration is the Earth considered with all its outward extensions ending at the surrounding heaven, so that it has an outward *above* while its further *below* is assigned only by imagination. The author thus rejects careless inference from the correlativity of a thing and its reference point to the correlativity of two opposed directions.

### Three principal accounts of the world's duration

Another property is that bodies are **originated in time** (*muḥdatha bi-l-zamān*). Three basic possibilities are distinguished:

1. Bodies and their attributes are both originated. This is the position of adherents of the religious communities, including Muslims.
2. Bodies and their attributes are beginningless. This is associated with Aristotle and his school. Here *attributes* includes forms as well as accidents. Celestial bodies are said to have beginningless matter and form, luminosity, figure and one continuous general motion and disposition—yet each individual part of that everlasting motion is preceded by another and is thus originated. Elemental bodies are beginningless in their prime matter and corporeal form, and in their being **some element** generically; the persistence from eternity of each particular fiery, airy, watery or earthy form is not thereby required, since those are subject to generation and corruption.
3. The basic substances are beginningless but their attributes originated. Various early philosophers are said to have held this, although they disagreed about the alleged primordial substance. Some took it to be bodily: all four elements, one from which the others arise by rarefaction and condensation, a distinctive original stuff producing both heavens and elements, or small hard bodies divisible in conception but not by actual cutting, sometimes supposed round and sometimes polygonal. Others took it as nonbodily: light and darkness whose mixture forms the world; soul and matter entering into relation; or unextended unities taking on location as points, with points assembling into lines, lines into surfaces and surfaces into bodies. The author treats some ancient formulations as symbolic or allusive rather than straightforward demonstrations. The reverse proposal—attributes beginningless but their subjects originated—is unintelligible.

### The standard proof: a body cannot be devoid of originated things

The famous syllogism is that **every body is inseparable from originated things**, and whatever is inseparable from originated things is itself originated. The minor premise is established in two ways.

On the first approach, bodies cannot be devoid of accidents, and **all accidents are originated**. Were an accident beginningless, it would remain, since on the assumptions already discussed what is eternal cannot perish; yet the earlier proofs purported to show that accidents of every kind do not persist. Therefore none is beginningless.

On the second, a body cannot be without **motion or rest**, for its being in a region is either preceded by being in a different region, in which case it is motion, or is not so preceded, in which case it is rest. Motion is originated because it is a transition from one condition to another, or one location after another, in a temporal succession where the earlier and later do not coexist. To be thus preceded is to have had an absence, and this is what temporal origination means here. Further, motion necessarily passes away, being a successive change; what can perish cannot be beginningless, on the relevant principles. Rest likewise is a **positive mode of being located**, capable of ceasing because every body admits movement. The latter may be grounded either in what the philosophers themselves allow, or in the sameness of bodies (what is possible for one is possible for all), or in the ability of parts of a homogeneous body to occupy one another's regions, and of adjacent parts of a compound to make contact through other surfaces. The qualification *positive* is significant: the nonexistence of an originated thing may precede it without itself being an eternal positive being. An argument from the impossibility of a beginningless entity's destruction concerns **existents**.

**Objections.** The first body at the first moment of its existence could not yet be moving or resting under these definitions, because each seems to require a preceding location. Also a mode of occupation which is not preceded by occupation of the **same** region is not necessarily motion: it might never have been preceded by occupation of **another** region. An eternal state cannot be preceded in that temporal fashion.

**Reply.** The argument concerns occupation preceded by a prior occupation. A first, wholly unprecedented occupation is already granted to be originated, which suffices for the intended result. Where there is a previous occupation, if it is in the present region the body is at rest; if it is in another it is moving. Eternal existence does not mean existence in a privileged first *instant* called “eternity.” It means absence of any first instant, or indefinitely prior continuation in whatever past times one supposes, just as everlastingness signifies continuation without a last future limit. The claim that a body is beginningless therefore cannot escape the movement/rest alternative by assigning its state to a special first instant beyond time.

### The deeper objection: a beginningless succession of originated motions

The philosophers do not require that **an individual motion** be beginningless. They can grant that every particular revolution, position or temporal part begins and ends, while maintaining that there is **no first** such part. The earlier syllogism then needs its major premise qualified: a thing which is never free of originated things need not itself originate unless the originating companions are **finite in number** or cannot succeed one another without beginning. It is therefore necessary to establish the impossibility of an infinite regress of successive originated events, not merely the origination of each event separately.

Two replies attempt to prove that **motion as a nature** cannot be beginningless. First, what is beginningless is not preceded by anything, while being preceded by one state and passing to another is integral to motion; the contrary of a necessary property is contrary to its subject. Second, if the nature of motion existed from eternity, some particular motion would have to be eternal because a universal does not exist externally except in an individual; yet the individual temporal parts are admittedly originated. These arguments require scrutiny: the opponent distinguishes a continuously instantiated kind from any one beginningless instance.

Two familiar demonstrations then attack beginningless succession itself. The **correspondence argument** imagines two sequences of earlier events, one counted backward from the present and the other backward from the Flood. If both have no beginning, an imagined alignment of their first counted members must either make the whole and its proper part equal or reveal that the shorter sequence ends, forcing the longer to end. The **correlativity argument** considers priority and posteriority. If a sequence contains an event which is preceded by another and does not precede a third—like a last effect—then, because “predecessor” and “successor” are correlative, the arrangement allegedly requires a counterpart which precedes without itself being preceded: a first event. Another formulation aligns a succession of being-preceded with one of preceding, seeking an unmatched first predecessor. These are versions of arguments encountered previously, and their premises concerning correspondence and infinite collections remain disputable.

### Additional proofs and their criticisms

Several other attempts are reported, with objections often immediately following. **(a)** If each event begins, the totality must begin, as though saying that every member of a group is black entails that the group is black. The inference is contested: the group is not itself just one member, and what is distributively true of the members need not be true of their totality. **(b)** An infinite succession allows addition or subtraction: more revolutions have occurred between the present and an imagined beginningless past than between the Flood and the present; similarly the sun's revolutions differ from Saturn's, and the number of days exceeds the numbers of months and years. Everything admitting addition or diminution is said to be finite. The counterargument distinguishes subtracting a finite number **at a finite end** from finding an unmatched member at the alleged infinite end. Even an infinite numerical series may differ by some additional members without thereby having an initial point.

**(c)** An infinite past cannot have been *completed*, whereas today requires that the past be over. The reply denies the inference: only a series which must be completed from its **infinite end** cannot be traversed to completion; the alleged endless past has no such first terminal end. **(d)** Every individual part of motion is an effect of a **voluntary agent** rather than a necessitating cause, because each part passes away while its supposed sufficient necessitating cause, if it persisted, would not allow that effect to cease. As the producer of every part produces the whole, motion must be originated. The opponent replies that a beginningless necessary cause might give rise to successive events through **newly arisen conditions**, each event depending on the cessation of a predecessor. A series of new conditions is precisely the point under dispute; restating that its individual members originate does not prove it begins.

**(e)** Either every motion is preceded by a different motion, in which case no *particular* one is eternal, or some motion is unpreceded and is the first. The philosopher chooses the first branch and again distinguishes each member's origination from a first member's existence. **(f)** Every event has a prior *beginningless nonexistence*. It is claimed that all these eternities of nonexistence must coincide in “eternity”; if any existence also obtains there, contradictories coexist, and if none obtains, motion must begin. The response is that **eternity is not a temporal container** within which all nonexistences are collected. To call an event's earlier absence beginningless is merely to say that it was not preceded by its own occurrence. It does not give all such absences one simultaneous temporal location. One cannot reason about an infinity of these absences as though they were a finite group whose items all had to be found at some common instant.

*Editorial note:* The argument's most important distinction is between (i) *each* motion beginning, (ii) the *kind* of motion being beginningless by successive instantiation, and (iii) an allegedly completed actual infinite series. The author reports and evaluates different defenses rather than suppressing the opponent's distinction.

On the second, a body cannot be without motion or rest, for its being in a region is either preceded by being in a different region, in which case it is motion, or is not so preceded, in which case it is rest. Motion is originated because it is a transition from one condition to another, or one location after another, in a temporal succession where the earlier and later do not coexist. To be thus preceded is to have had an absence, and this is what temporal origination means here. Further, motion necessarily passes away, being a successive change; what can perish cannot be beginningless, on the relevant principles. Rest likewise is a positive mode of being located, capable of ceasing because every body admits movement. The latter may be grounded either in what the philosophers themselves allow, or in the sameness of bodies (what is possible for one is possible for all), or in the ability of parts of a homogeneous body to occupy one another's regions, and of adjacent parts of a compound to make contact through other surfaces. The qualification positive is significant: the nonexistence of an originated thing may precede it without itself being an eternal positive being. An argument from the impossibility of a beginningless entity's destruction concerns existents.

Objections. The first body at the first moment of its existence could not yet be moving or resting under these definitions, because each seems to require a preceding location. Also a mode of occupation which is not preceded by occupation of the same region is not necessarily motion: it might never have been preceded by occupation of another region. An eternal state cannot be preceded in that temporal fashion.

Reply. The argument concerns occupation preceded by a prior occupation. A first, wholly unprecedented occupation is already granted to be originated, which suffices for the intended result. Where there is a previous occupation, if it is in the present region the body is at rest; if it is in another it is moving. Eternal existence does not mean existence in a privileged first instant called “eternity.” It means absence of any first instant, or indefinitely prior continuation in whatever past times one supposes, just as everlastingness signifies continuation without a last future limit. The claim that a body is beginningless therefore cannot escape the movement/rest alternative by assigning its state to a special first instant beyond time.

The deeper objection: a beginningless succession of originated motions

The philosophers do not require that an individual motion be beginningless. They can grant that every particular revolution, position or temporal part begins and ends, while maintaining that there is no first such part. The earlier syllogism then needs its major premise qualified: a thing which is never free of originated things need not itself originate unless the originating companions are finite in number or cannot succeed one another without beginning. It is therefore necessary to establish the impossibility of an infinite regress of successive originated events, not merely the origination of each event separately.

Two replies attempt to prove that motion as a nature cannot be beginningless. First, what is beginningless is not preceded by anything, while being preceded by one state and passing to another is integral to motion; the contrary of a necessary property is contrary to its subject. Second, if the nature of motion existed from eternity, some particular motion would have to be eternal because a universal does not exist externally except in an individual; yet the individual temporal parts are admittedly originated. These arguments require scrutiny: the opponent distinguishes a continuously instantiated kind from any one beginningless instance.

Two familiar demonstrations then attack beginningless succession itself. The correspondence argument imagines two sequences of earlier events, one counted backward from the present and the other backward from the Flood. If both have no beginning, an imagined alignment of their first counted members must either make the whole and its proper part equal or reveal that the shorter sequence ends, forcing the longer to end. The correlativity argument considers priority and posteriority. If a sequence contains an event which is preceded by another and does not precede a third—like a last effect—then, because “predecessor” and “successor” are correlative, the arrangement allegedly requires a counterpart which precedes without itself being preceded: a first event. Another formulation aligns a succession of being-preceded with one of preceding, seeking an unmatched first predecessor. These are versions of arguments encountered previously, and their premises concerning correspondence and infinite collections remain disputable.

Additional proofs and their criticisms

Several other attempts are reported, with objections often immediately following. (a) If each event begins, the totality must begin, as though saying that every member of a group is black entails that the group is black. The inference is contested: the group is not itself just one member, and what is distributively true of the members need not be true of their totality. (b) An infinite succession allows addition or subtraction: more revolutions have occurred between the present and an imagined beginningless past than between the Flood and the present; similarly the sun's revolutions differ from Saturn's, and the number of days exceeds the numbers of months and years. Everything admitting addition or diminution is said to be finite. The counterargument distinguishes subtracting a finite number at a finite end from finding an unmatched member at the alleged infinite end. Even an infinite numerical series may differ by some additional members without thereby having an initial point.

(c) An infinite past cannot have been completed, whereas today requires that the past be over. The reply denies the inference: only a series which must be completed from its infinite end cannot be traversed to completion; the alleged endless past has no such first terminal end. (d) Every individual part of motion is an effect of a voluntary agent rather than a necessitating cause, because each part passes away while its supposed sufficient necessitating cause, if it persisted, would not allow that effect to cease. As the producer of every part produces the whole, motion must be originated. The opponent replies that a beginningless necessary cause might give rise to successive events through newly arisen conditions, each event depending on the cessation of a predecessor. The philosopher chooses the first branch and again distinguishes each member's origination from a first member's existence. (f) Every event has a prior beginningless nonexistence. It is claimed that all these eternities of nonexistence must coincide in “eternity”; if any existence also obtains there, contradictories coexist, and if none obtains, motion must begin. The response is that eternity is not a temporal container within which all nonexistences are collected. To call an event's earlier absence beginningless is merely to say that it was not preceded by its own occurrence. It does not give all such absences one simultaneous temporal location. One cannot reason about an infinity of these absences as though they were a finite group whose items all had to be found at some common instant.

The author reports and evaluates different defenses rather than suppressing the opponent's distinction.

# MQ-C04-016 — Additional demonstrations of origination; objections for the eternity of the world

**Arabic source:** source characters 799973–807664, printed markers I.330–333. **Status:** close explanatory translation, with an electronic text-displacement flagged near I.333.

### A shortened argument from states of being-located

If one did not wish to answer particular schools of earlier philosophers in detail, the argument for bodily origination could be shorter. Some philosophers maintained beginningless celestial motions, with each motion preceded by another; others posited beginningless minute solid bodies which originally stood still and later moved and assembled into composites; still others thought that primordial bodies moved, collided and stopped, thereby producing the heavens and the elements. Against these particular opinions, the discussion considered whether rest is a positive attribute and whether a body is necessarily attended by motion or rest. But a more general formulation needs only the doctrine of **being-located** (*kawn*).

If anything bodily were beginningless, then either some state of its being-located would itself be beginningless, or there would be an endless succession of states without a first. It is necessary that a body have some manner of occupation of a region: when the mind conceives a spatially extended substance, it judges that it has such a mode of occupancy. A state of occupancy is either eternal or preceded by another state. The first branch is excluded, it is said, because a body can move from one region to another, whether wholly as in rectilinear motion or through movement of its parts as in circular motion. Hence every individual state of occupation can disappear, whereas nothing whose nonexistence is possible is beginningless, on the principle that what is truly beginningless cannot cease. The second branch is excluded by the correspondence proof, the argument from correlative priority/posteriority, and the other anti-regress demonstrations already considered. Thus the body has a beginning.

### Other proofs for bodily origination

**Second proof:** bodies are **subjects of originated things**, as observation testifies, and no beginningless being can receive them. If the claim that bodies receive new accidents were only particular, it would prove the origination of some bodies, which no one denies for common elemental composites. To establish all bodies' origination, the minor premise must be universal: celestial and elementary bodies alike are affected by new motion and new disposition, while the elements additionally take on varying illumination and other states. Origination of the simple substances would entail the origination of their composites.

**Third proof:** every body is possible and thus depends upon an influence or producer. The sequence of dependent causes must terminate in the **Necessary Existent**. As will be established in the Divine Matters division, the Maker acts **by choice**, and an effect of a voluntary agent is originated and preceded by the intention of producing it; such intention concerns its production when it was absent. This establishes the origination of all entities other than the Maker, bodies and accidents alike, without applying it to the Maker's own eternal attributes. The argument works, however, only on a doctrine making **mere possibility** sufficient to require an efficient cause. A related fourth proof avoids the proof that the Maker chooses, but relies on the familiar claim that causing a thing when it already exists would be *obtaining what is already obtained* (*taḥṣīl al-ḥāṣil*), an equivocation previously answered.

**Fifth proof:** a body necessarily possesses a determinate measure and region. Both are supposedly originated, since an agent which acts by necessary efflux would relate equally to all quantities and places, and only a chooser could assign this particular one. But the conclusion can be contested: the special measure or location may result from matter, form, the number of indivisible atoms, or further external causes. It is not enough simply to assert the equal relation of a necessitating cause.

**Another proposed proof:** if body were beginningless, its *eternity* would be additional to its essence because eternity is a concept common to body and the Necessary. Either the eternity of this eternity is eternal, generating a regress, or it is originated, which makes the alleged eternal body originated. This is plainly weak. Eternity can be a **rational consideration**, not an independently existing attribute whose eternity needs a further eternal property. In any case the eternity of eternity may be identical with it. By parity, if an originated body's origination had to be an additional entity, one might ask whether that origination itself were originated or eternal and raise an equally defective regress.

### Philosophers' defenses of an eternal world

The first and best-known argument for the world's eternity begins with **all that is required for its production**. Either every prerequisite obtains in eternity or something required comes into existence later. The second branch, it is argued, generates a regress: if a condition itself appears later, all the conditions needed for *its* appearance either preexist or depend on a further appearing condition. The first branch appears to entail that the world also exists from eternity, because a complete necessitating cause cannot exist without its effect.

**General reply:** this reasoning would also prove that no ordinary event which happens today can be originated; it could be repeated verbatim concerning the conditions for that event. **Philosophers' answer:** present-day events depend on renewed dispositions in matter, produced by successive celestial motions, positions and conjunctions. Each condition arrives after the earlier one has ceased; these preparatory conditions are not a regress of simultaneously ordered efficient causes. **Counterreply:** several anti-regress demonstrations already proposed, including correspondence and priority/posteriority, are intended also to exclude succession; and if successive events can condition the material world's events, why could an origination of the corporeal world not follow a succession of perceptions, volitions or other occurrences in an immaterial being? The philosophers deny such succession among immaterials by invoking the maxim that every originated event requires matter and time, but that maxim has already been questioned.

**More precise reply:** the sufficiency of every prerequisite from eternity does not compel the world's eternal existence if one of the prerequisites is **will**, whose very function is to select and specify one alternative at a chosen time without an extrinsic determining condition. The philosophers protest that an effect's absence despite its complete cause is an impossible absence of necessitation, or an ungrounded preference. The theologian responds that this assumes the causation of a choosing will works like that of a necessitating cause. A chooser selects one of two equally accessible pieces of bread, or one of two paths of escape, without needing an additional external cause to make the selection. One might further object that bare eternal will is insufficient: its specific **relation to its object** (*taʿalluq*) must occur, and that relation either is eternal, forcing the effect to be eternal, or originates without a cause. The answer treats that relational specification as something occurring through will, not through a distinct external condition. The theologian consequently accepts the possibility that a complete cause **including choice** does not necessitate an immediate simultaneous effect.

**Second argument:** the world's possibility is eternal, and the Maker's power to produce it is eternally applicable. If it were impossible in eternity and then became possible, there would be a change from impossibility into possibility. Why, then, would the all-generous agent withhold His beneficence for an infinite period? **Reply:** even granting the ethical premise concerning generosity, this inference conflates two propositions: that existence is **eternally possible** (*al-imkān azalan*) and that an existent can be placed **in eternity as a temporal container** (*al-wujūd fī l-azal*). A created thing, precisely as created, may always have been possible, while its existence with no beginning remains contradictory to its being created. The eternity of a modal possibility does not imply actual temporal eternity of its object.

**Third argument:** philosophers appeal to prime matter and corporeal form, alleged to be eternal and inseparable. Their premises have been contested in the preceding investigations.

**Fourth argument:** the body-associated **time**, conceived as the measure of motion, must be beginningless. If time originated, its preceding nonexistence could not have preceded it through causation, rank, honor or nature; it would therefore precede **in time**, absurdly requiring another time in which time itself was absent. **Reply:** even if time is real and is measured by motion, the alleged list of kinds of priority is incomplete. The priority of yesterday over tomorrow, which belongs to successive temporal parts, cannot be explained by inserting **another time** in which both yesterday and tomorrow coexist. The priority of time's nonexistence to its existence can likewise be understood without making it a preceding event contained in already existing time. title: The outermost sphere as determiner of directions (vol. I, pp. 333–336)
en:
**First subdivision: simple celestial bodies.** The first enquiry is whether one spherical body surrounds all others and determines the two principal directions, above and below; it is called **the determiner of directions** (*muḥaddid al-jihāt*). The philosophical proof assumes that directions are real termini or limits of extensions, have determinate positions, and that above and below are fixed opposing directions. A bodily reference must establish their positions. It must be one spherical body encompassing the whole: “above” is determined by the nearest limit of its outer circumference, and “below” by the farthest limit, its centre.

It must be a body, they say, because only what has position can determine a position. It must be **one**: if two distinct bodies determine directions, either one contains the other, in which case only the outermost provides the final terminus, or neither contains the other, in which case each occupies some direction relative to the other and thus presupposes rather than originates directions. A further argument says each would determine only the side of nearness, leaving its opposite indeterminate. The commentator questions that second inference: two appropriately placed bodies could each mark both extreme proximity to itself and extreme remoteness from the other. The first argument is preferred.

It is said to be **spherical and simple**, incapable of departure from its natural circular form. If it were composite, its parts would have to combine through straight motions and remain separable. If a simple body lost its natural sphericity, it would likewise admit straight displacement. But straight motion requires a prior distinction of places and directions, whereas directions are supposed to be determined by this very body. For a composite, the possibility of separation follows from essentially similar constituents meeting different neighbours on their different sides; what meets a neighbour on one side could be moved to meet it on the other. The author objects that this would show only that *directions precede the assembly and motion of parts*, not that they precede the composite body as presently constituted. Thus this proof does not establish the determiner's simplicity.

Two alternative arguments for its **roundness** are also rejected. First, a nonspherical body is said to determine only proximity, not absolute remoteness. But an oval, lens-shaped or even polygonal body has an interior point most distant from its boundary in the relevant respect; unequal radial distances alone do not destroy a determinate centre. Second, a nonspherical outermost body revolving around something round is said to leave temporary empty gaps between their surfaces; but an outer shell with a circular inner surface and an elliptical outer one could rotate in a way that avoids such gaps. If its specific nature is invoked to prove that the *outer surface* too must be round, that is a separate argument and not a proof from rotation and unavoidable vacuum. Geometric terms for oval and lens-shaped surfaces are explained by their generating arcs, although the decisive issue is that geometry alone does not exclude the countermodels.

Why must the determiner **encompass** all situated things? A smaller body marks merely nearness to itself, not the final limits of directional extension. A conceptual objection asks whether it *efficiently causes* direction or *receives* it. On the first account, why must it be situated and all-encompassing? On the second, the upper and lower limits are not received by a single body, since the lower centre lies within the earth. The reply says the “determiner” is neither an efficient maker of directions nor a material bearer of their limits. It is **that through reference to which their position becomes determinate**. The centre counts as “below” not because it is a point of earth as earth, but because it is the centre of the encompassing heavenly sphere. A given circumference determines its centre, while the same given centre could be surrounded by indefinitely many possible circumferences. The sphere, not the earth, is therefore the ultimate directional reference.

It is objected that each elemental region might be bounded by its own containing sphere; the natural place of fire is supposedly the concave surface of the moon's sphere, not the outermost heaven, suggesting the moon's sphere determines fire's “above.” The answer sharply distinguishes **direction** (*jiha*) from **place** (*makān*). Place is the immediate containing surface touching the contained body, while absolute direction is the terminal point of all outward extension. The moon's sphere provides the *natural place* of fire, not the metaphysical limit of “above.” Fire naturally seeks its proper region, not the outermost directional limit itself. Even if fire were imagined as passing through the sphere of the moon, its motion would remain *upward*, rather than from an already completed “above.” Ordinary phrases about seeking “the upper direction” therefore refer loosely to the place adjoining that direction.

A further dispute concerns whether parts of the outermost sphere are themselves above and below in the same way as parts of other spheres. Some allow an inner and outer side, with the convex outer surface higher and concave inner surface lower, taking the external limit as the actual determiner. Others insist the entire outermost sphere is “above” intrinsically, whereas the earth is “below” only because it lies at the centre; if the earth moved away from the centre its motion would be upward from below. These distinctions depend upon how the determining reference is understood.

**The commentator's theological evaluation.** The philosophical proof relies on denying the possibility of void, since if a void were possible a line might terminate in a position without any encompassing body, and on holding that different bodies have intrinsically different natures and naturally compelled directions of motion. The theologians do **not** grant these premises: void is possible; bodies are essentially alike, even if their accidents differ; and motions are effects of the power of a freely choosing agent, not necessary operations of bodily natures. Consequently they reject the alleged demonstration of a determiner, and with it the inference that the heavens cannot move in straight lines.

Nor does the doctrine establish that the heavens cannot be broken, separated and rejoined, generated or destroyed, heated or cooled, moist or dry, coloured, flavoured or fragrant, soft or hard, smooth or rough, light or heavy. Such sweeping exclusions are also at odds with religious descriptions of transformation in the heavens. Even on the philosophical premises, the proof would apply primarily to the proposed *outermost* directional body, not to every internal sphere. Observed circular motions do not establish the impossibility of **their cessation and replacement by straight motion**; still less do they show that motion is intrinsically perpetual, especially when the philosophers themselves regard celestial movement as voluntary rather than an inseparable natural attribute. Ancient spiritual philosophers are also reported as describing very hard, dry and smooth spheres whose contact during their revolutions produces extraordinary musical harmonies heard by spiritually trained persons. The commentator records the report without allowing it to supply proof.

A conceptual objection asks whether it efficiently causes direction or receives it. On the first account, why must it be situated and all-encompassing? On the second, the upper and lower limits are not received by a single body, since the lower centre lies within the earth. The centre counts as “below” not because it is a point of earth as earth, but because it is the centre of the encompassing heavenly sphere. A given circumference determines its centre, while the same given centre could be surrounded by indefinitely many possible circumferences. The sphere, not the earth, is therefore the ultimate directional reference.

It is objected that each elemental region might be bounded by its own containing sphere; the natural place of fire is supposedly the concave surface of the moon's sphere, not the outermost heaven, suggesting the moon's sphere determines fire's “above.” The answer sharply distinguishes direction (jiha) from place (makān). Place is the immediate containing surface touching the contained body, while absolute direction is the terminal point of all outward extension. The moon's sphere provides the natural place of fire, not the metaphysical limit of “above.” Fire naturally seeks its proper region, not the outermost directional limit itself. Even if fire were imagined as passing through the sphere of the moon, its motion would remain upward, rather than from an already completed “above.” Ordinary phrases about seeking “the upper direction” therefore refer loosely to the place adjoining that direction.

A further dispute concerns whether parts of the outermost sphere are themselves above and below in the same way as parts of other spheres. Some allow an inner and outer side, with the convex outer surface higher and concave inner surface lower, taking the external limit as the actual determiner. Others insist the entire outermost sphere is “above” intrinsically, whereas the earth is “below” only because it lies at the centre; if the earth moved away from the centre its motion would be upward from below. These distinctions depend upon how the determining reference is understood.

The commentator's theological evaluation. The philosophical proof relies on denying the possibility of void, since if a void were possible a line might terminate in a position without any encompassing body, and on holding that different bodies have intrinsically different natures and naturally compelled directions of motion. The theologians do not grant these premises: void is possible; bodies are essentially alike, even if their accidents differ; and motions are effects of the power of a freely choosing agent, not necessary operations of bodily natures. Consequently they reject the alleged demonstration of a determiner, and with it the inference that the heavens cannot move in straight lines.

Nor does the doctrine establish that the heavens cannot be broken, separated and rejoined, generated or destroyed, heated or cooled, moist or dry, coloured, flavoured or fragrant, soft or hard, smooth or rough, light or heavy. Such sweeping exclusions are also at odds with religious descriptions of transformation in the heavens. Even on the philosophical premises, the proof would apply primarily to the proposed outermost directional body, not to every internal sphere. Observed circular motions do not establish the impossibility of their cessation and replacement by straight motion; still less do they show that motion is intrinsically perpetual, especially when the philosophers themselves regard celestial movement as voluntary rather than an inseparable natural attribute. Ancient spiritual philosophers are also reported as describing very hard, dry and smooth spheres whose contact during their revolutions produces extraordinary musical harmonies heard by spiritually trained persons. title: Spheres, epicycles, eclipses, and the received astronomical model (vol. I, pp. 336–340)
en:
**Second investigation: a survey of mathematical astronomy.** The exposition now includes much of *ʿilm al-hayʾa*, the study of the magnitudes, qualities, positions and motions of upper and lower simple bodies. Some of its findings are useful in religious law and observance: differences in rising and setting points, the direction of prayer and the times of prayer. Others encourage reflection on the creation of heaven and earth and thus knowledge of the maker's wisdom and power. Still others are to be reported precisely in order to identify possible errors. This science normally presupposes a separate mathematical work, the *Almagest*, where its proofs are elaborated. A faithful summary is legitimate, but the commentator criticizes inaccurate summaries, including passages in *al-Mawāqif*, which allow astronomers to reproach theologians for insufficient knowledge of the art.

The astronomers observed the ordinary daily movement of the sun, moon and stars from east to west, a slower apparent west-to-east displacement discernible through accurate observation, and seven wandering bodies—sun, moon, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury—with distinctive movements that differ from one another. Assuming stars to be fixed into their rotating spheres rather than swimming through them like fish in water, and denying that a single simple sphere can undergo two genuinely different motions at the same time, they proposed **nine principal encompassing spheres** centred on the earth: two accounting for the general and slower motions and seven for the distinct motions of the planets. The number is not a demonstrated maximum: every fixed star could conceivably have its own sphere, and many unstarred spheres could contain one another; they rejected excess spheres for lack of evidence and because astronomy ought not to posit needless machinery. Some accept eight spheres and attribute the first motion to the combined system through one moving soul. The author of the *Tuḥfa* even allows seven, treating the fixed-star paths as part of Saturn's outer boundary and assigning one universal daily motion alongside a different motion of the seventh sphere, with suitable assumptions about the zodiacal reference points.

To call the highest sphere unstarred and moving is an assumption of the model, not one shared by theorists who allow stars to float within spheres. Its great circle is called the **equator of day and night** (*muʿaddil al-nahār*) because day and night are equal when the sun lies on the corresponding celestial circle. The *zone* or equatorial great circle of a sphere is generated by its rotation; its two **poles** are the stationary points of the rotation, and parallel smaller circles its **circles of rotation**. The pole to the north of a person facing east is the northern pole, the other southern. The general revolution is completed in **approximately** a day and night, since the sun's own slow eastward motion makes the ordinary solar day slightly longer than the full celestial revolution. The ninth sphere is said to carry all eight within it, as though they formed a single sphere under its dominance. Yet motion of a containing body does not strictly force an enclosed body to share its angular motion unless the enclosed body is physically part of the enclosing shell, as happens with the eccentric embedded in its deferent.

The **eighth sphere** contains the so-called fixed stars other than the seven wanderers. They are “fixed” either because their motion is extraordinarily slow or because the angular separations between them and their distances from the poles of their own rotating sphere remain approximately unchanged. Astronomers assign the eighth sphere a different axis and equator from those of the ninth. If both rotated around the very same axis, observation could distinguish only the net faster or slower rotation, or no motion if they exactly balanced. Observational instruments were used to infer a separate axis from changes measured relative to the fixed stars. Ancient estimates differed: Ptolemy and earlier astronomers assigned one degree per hundred years, or a full circuit in 36,000 years; later estimates gave one degree per sixty-six years, roughly 23,760 years for a revolution; another gave one degree in seventy years, about 25,200 years, a figure connected with Marāgha observations. Differences could reflect instrumental inaccuracies or causes ultimately known only to the creator.

**Evidence for planetary order from occultations and parallax.** The moon is seen to obscure other wandering bodies and some fixed stars along its path, so its sphere is placed below them. Similar comparisons determine much of the ordering. The sun is obscured by the moon, but small stars are not readily seen transiting it because their light is overwhelmed when they approach it. The placement of the sun above Venus and Mercury was therefore often a matter of aesthetic arrangement: the greatest luminary is made the centre of the sequence of wanderers, as the prominent gem in a necklace, and the ordering has other supposed harmonies. There are reports of Venus seen crossing the solar disc, but they were not generally conclusive. The sun is placed below Saturn, Jupiter and Mars through **parallax**, the difference between the lines from the world's centre and the observer's location toward an object. Observable parallax marks relative nearness, its absence greater distance. Astronomers detected it for the sun but not for the three superior planets or fixed stars. Mercury and Venus are difficult to observe high at the meridian while visible because they remain close to the sun; the special two-pronged instrument used for parallax cannot easily settle their order. Since the model does not insist on precisely one sphere per fixed star, it is no objection merely to note that some could lie below or among the wandering planets without disturbing the phenomena.

**Deferents, eccentric spheres, and epicycles.** The principal sphere or *representative* (*mumaththil*) of a wandering planet is called such because its centre, equator and poles correspond to the zodiacal reference sphere. Observed irregularities require subordinate spheres. For the moon the representative is called *jawzaharī* because it carries the lunar nodes; inside it lies an **inclined** (*māʾil*) sphere centred on the world but with its equatorial great circle at a fixed inclination to the zodiac. The outer lunar sphere is adjacent above to Mercury's representative sphere and below to the inclined sphere, which in turn reaches the outer limit of the sphere of fire.

An **eccentric** (*khārij al-markaz*) is a spherical shell whose centre does not coincide with the earth's centre but lies within a concentric representative sphere, touching that sphere at the point farthest from the earth, the **apogee** (*awj*), and at the opposite point nearest the earth, the **perigee** (*ḥaḍīḍ*). The portions of the representative shell remaining on either side of the eccentric form two complementary shells (*mutammimāt*), thickest where the eccentric is farthest from their boundary and tapering toward points of tangency. Their respective thick and thin regions alternate. An eccentric may itself be fitted inside another eccentric, as in the model of Mercury.

An **epicycle** (*tadwīr*) is a small solid sphere embedded in the thickness of the eccentric *deferent* (*ḥāmil*) and tangent at its upper and lower extremes, traditionally called its summit and nadir; the planet is fixed within the epicycle, itself treated as solid rather than hollow. The moon's concentric representative contains an inclined sphere, inside which its eccentric deferent carries the lunar epicycle. Mercury's representative contains a first eccentric, the **director** (*mudīr*), and that contains a second eccentric, the deferent carrying Mercury's epicycle; Mercury thus has two eccentrics, two apogees, two perigees and four complementary shells. The sun's representative contains one eccentric on which the sun itself is located. Each of the four remaining planets has a representative containing an eccentric deferent, whose epicycle bears the planet. These elaborate arrangements purport to describe the observed combinations of planetary motions rather than the independently established real constitution of heaven.

title: Zodiacal division, planetary periods, and elementary motions (vol. I, pp. 340–343)
en:
**Third investigation.** Since the ecliptic, or zodiacal circle (*minṭaqat al-burūj*), and the celestial equator (*muʿaddil al-nahār*) intersect at two points, the astronomers imagine a circle passing through the two intersections and through the two zodiacal poles, and another passing through all four poles, cutting both great circles at right angles. At the latter intersection the distance between the two circles reaches its maximum, called the **total obliquity** (*al-mayl al-kullī*). These imaginary circles divide the ecliptic into four equal quarters. By marking two corresponding points on each of two adjacent quarters and drawing four further circles through these and the corresponding points opposite, they obtain six great circles which cut the encompassing heaven into twelve equal divisions, the **signs** (*burūj*). Each sign is divided into thirty degrees; each degree into sixty minutes, each minute into sixty seconds and each second into sixty thirds, with the sexagesimal subdivision continuing indefinitely.

Of the two equinoctial intersections, the point at which the sun crosses into the north of the equator is called the **vernal equinox**, and that at which it crosses toward the south is the **autumnal equinox**. The intersection of the ecliptic with the circle passing through the four poles on the northern side is the **summer solstice**, and the corresponding southern intersection the **winter solstice**. Spring denotes the time in which the sun travels from the northward crossing to the northern solstice, across Aries, Taurus and Gemini; summer is its passage through Cancer, Leo and Virgo to the southward crossing; autumn its course through Libra, Scorpio and Sagittarius to the southern solstice; winter its course through Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces back to the vernal equinox. The names of the signs were drawn from figures imagined among the stars lying opposite the sections at the original division. Though the motion of the eighth sphere subsequently carried those stars away from the positions to which the signs were originally referred, the names were retained for convenience in recording celestial motions.

**The planets' passage through the signs.** Each of the wandering stars passes through the zodiacal signs successively from Aries to Taurus, Gemini and onward: that direction is *with the order* (*ʿalā al-tawālī*), from west to east; proceeding from Aries to Pisces to Aquarius and so forth is *against the order* (*ʿalā khilāf al-tawālī*). In this general account, “motion” means the composite apparent movement by which a planet changes its zodiacal sign, without resolving the motion into its component spheres. The detailed account, by contrast, treats those separate rotations. The sun traverses the twelve signs in about 365¼ days, the solar year; the moon does so twelve times in approximately 354 days and a fraction, the lunar year; Saturn in about thirty years, Jupiter in twelve, Mars in a little less than two, and Venus and Mercury each in roughly one. These are approximations; precision is sought from astronomical tables (*zījes*).

The detail distinguishes particular rotations moving **against** the order from those moving **with** it. Mercury's *mudabbir* sphere rotates about its own centre on a plane oblique to both the equator and the ecliptic and with poles different from both; its effects appear in the apogee and perigee of the deferent. It carries the deferent's centre around the *mudabbir*'s centre, forming the so-called sphere carrying the centre of the deferent, at the specified daily rate of 59 minutes, 8 seconds and 20 thirds. The commentator says the mode of discovering this sphere and the direction and magnitude of its movement are familiar in the astronomical literature. He corrects three slips in the account in *al-Mawāqif*: the Mercury epicycle's centre and the deferent's apogee are said there to stand opposite one another in Libra and Aries, whereas the relevant placement is conjunction, not opposition; *mudabbir* properly names the mover of the deferent's apogee, which in turn moves the epicycle's centre, rather than the direct mover of the epicycle's centre; and Mercury's greatest morning and evening separation from the sun is assigned to Libra rather than Aries, whereas the relation is the reverse.

Another retrograde component is the motion of the moon's **inclined representative sphere** (*mumaththil al-qamar*), around the centre of the world on the ecliptic and its poles, by three minutes and twelve seconds daily. All the lunar spheres participate in this movement, carrying the head and tail of the lunar nodes; it is thus attributed to the nodes and called the **motion of the jawzahar**. The moon's inclined sphere (*māʾil*) also moves about the world-centre on a plane distinct from the equator and ecliptic, at eleven degrees and nine minutes daily: this carries its eccentric sphere and centre, and is named the motion of the apogee, where it becomes apparent. Sometimes the sum of these two lunar movements is called the apogee's motion.

Among movements with the order are those of the representative spheres other than that of the moon. Their effects appear in the apogees and perigees and accord with the motion of the eighth heaven. Some therefore ascribe them to that sphere, while others attribute distinct motions to the representative spheres themselves so that the spheres do not remain idle; on the latter account it is denied that a containing body must move whatever is within it. Also moving with the order are the eccentric deferents, except Mercury's sphere specifically named *mudabbir*. The text gives their distinct daily rates—sun about 59′8″20‴, Saturn 2′, Jupiter 5′, Mars 31′, Venus the same as the sun, Mercury 1½°, and moon 24°23′—on their respective inclined planes. Their effect appears in the centres of the epicycles of the six planets, which explains the designation **motion of a planet's centre**. In the epicycles, the upper halves of those of the five wandering planets other than the moon move with the order, while for the moon it is the lower half. The daily epicyclic movement of each superior planet corresponds to the excess of solar motion over its deferent's motion; the stated rates for Venus, Mercury and the moon are 37′, 3°6′ and 13°4′ respectively. The opposite halves must accordingly move against the order.

**Celestial latitude and longitude.** The moon's epicycle moves in the plane of its deferent and inclined sphere; its departure from the ecliptic consequently arises only from the inclination of the lunar plane. For the five other planets their epicycles are inclined relative to their own deferents, which are themselves inclined to the ecliptic, so there can be one latitude due to the deferent's inclination and another due to the epicycle's inclination. *Latitude* (*ʿarḍ al-kawkab*) is the arc along the circle through the ecliptic's poles and through the direction from the world's centre toward the planet, between the ecliptic and that direction. It stands opposite *longitude* (*ṭūl*): the arc measured along the zodiac in the order of the signs from the vernal point to the planet if the latter has no latitude, or to the point where its latitude circle intersects the ecliptic if it does.

The intersections of an inclined orbital circle and its representative sphere are called the two **nodes** (*jawzaharān*). The one through which a planet crosses to the north is the **head** (*raʾs*), its opposite the **tail** (*dhanab*). The terminology pictures a dragon formed by the narrow areas enclosed between the intersecting circles; north is described as the head because of its supposed superiority, the visibility of the northern pole and the distribution of inhabited lands and stars. The lunar inclined sphere and the eccentric spheres of the five other wandering planets are all oblique to the ecliptic, and hence each cuts its representative sphere at these nodes.

On that framework there are two spheres for the general motions and, for the sun, a representative sphere, eccentric and epicycle; for the moon, an inclined sphere, representative, eccentric and epicycle; for each superior planet and Venus, a representative, eccentric and epicycle; and for Mercury a representative, *mudabbir*, eccentric and epicycle. Counting the specified subordinate rotations, they arrive at **twenty-four partial celestial spheres and twenty-four corresponding simple motions**. This construction rests on the assumption that celestial movements are intrinsically uniform, without true stopping, reversal, acceleration, retardation or deviations from their ordained paths. When observation shows those appearances the astronomers multiply spheres and movements to explain them while maintaining each component's uniformity. Eccentrics and epicycles account for changes in apparent speed, and epicycles for apparent retrogression and station. These are models built to save the appearances under the uniform-motion principle, not themselves immediately observed bodies.

It stands opposite longitude (ṭūl): the arc measured along the zodiac in the order of the signs from the vernal point to the planet if the latter has no latitude, or to the point where its latitude circle intersects the ecliptic if it does.

The intersections of an inclined orbital circle and its representative sphere are called the two nodes (jawzaharān). The one through which a planet crosses to the north is the head (raʾs), its opposite the tail (dhanab). The terminology pictures a dragon formed by the narrow areas enclosed between the intersecting circles; north is described as the head because of its supposed superiority, the visibility of the northern pole and the distribution of inhabited lands and stars. The lunar inclined sphere and the eccentric spheres of the five other wandering planets are all oblique to the ecliptic, and hence each cuts its representative sphere at these nodes.

On that framework there are two spheres for the general motions and, for the sun, a representative sphere, eccentric and epicycle; for the moon, an inclined sphere, representative, eccentric and epicycle; for each superior planet and Venus, a representative, eccentric and epicycle; and for Mercury a representative, mudabbir, eccentric and epicycle. Counting the specified subordinate rotations, they arrive at twenty-four partial celestial spheres and twenty-four corresponding simple motions. This construction rests on the assumption that celestial movements are intrinsically uniform, without true stopping, reversal, acceleration, retardation or deviations from their ordained paths. When observation shows those appearances the astronomers multiply spheres and movements to explain them while maintaining each component's uniformity. Eccentrics and epicycles account for changes in apparent speed, and epicycles for apparent retrogression and station. These are models built to save the appearances under the uniform-motion principle, not themselves immediately observed bodies.

title: Apparent stations, retrogression, phases and eclipses; difficulties in the received models (vol. I, pp. 343–346)
en:
The differences in apparent planetary speed can arise when a body performs a uniform circular motion around a centre eccentric to the centre of our earth. The far portion of its path subtends a smaller visual arc than an equal portion of the nearer path. Draw the line joining the two centres and extending through apogee and perigee, then a perpendicular through the world's centre to the circuit. This divides the representative sphere into equal semicircles, but the eccentric circuit into unequal arcs: the arc lying in the apogeal half is longer and requires more time at uniform angular speed, while the arc in the perigeal half is shorter. Accordingly apparent motion is slowest in the former, fastest in the latter, and intermediate near the ends of the perpendicular. The analogy is with travelling two parasangs in one hour and only one in another: the apparent rates differ because the distances corresponding to a given direction differ. Thus the spring and summer solar seasons are longer than autumn and winter, although each pair represents passage through half the zodiac.

An epicycle furnishes the second explanation. When a planet lies on the half of its epicycle whose motion accords with that of the deferent (upper half for the five planets and lower half for the moon), the two motions reinforce one another, producing rapid apparent progress. In the opposite half, the epicycle subtracts from the deferent's movement. If it is slower than the deferent, the planet still advances but slowly; if exactly equal, its apparent zodiacal position remains fixed—the **station** (*wuqūf*); if the contrary epicyclic motion exceeds the deferent's motion, the planet appears to move backward—the **retrogradation** (*rujūʿ*). The condition of equality, it is argued, is available to the other wandering planets but not to the moon given the rates specified above. The figures are illustrative: the deferent might advance it one degree while the epicycle returns it two.

**Evidential status of the model.** An objection says that the inference from observed changes in longitude and speed to these particular eccentric spheres and epicycles is formally invalid: from a consequent one may not infer its antecedent unless their equivalence has been proved. The observations might have other causes, and neither self-evidence nor demonstration excludes that possibility. Astronomers answer that these are **intuitive judgements** (*muqaddamāt ḥadsiyya*): an intellect already convinced of celestial regularity finds the required arrangement immediately upon perceiving the differences, without explicitly arranging a middle term. They readily acknowledge this character of their reasoning in the cases of solar and lunar eclipses. Where no decisive intuitive judgement occurs they differ and hesitate—about the Milky Way, the dark markings on the moon, whether the sun's uneven apparent speed is due to eccentricity or an epicycle, and whether the motion of apogees originates in their respective representative spheres or is carried by the eighth heaven. The commentator reports this defence, without turning underdetermined model selection into a strict demonstration.

**The moon's borrowed light.** As an example of a famous inference, the changing apparent shape of the moon in relation to the sun indicates that its body is dark in itself, dense enough to receive sunlight and sufficiently smooth to reflect it. Since the sun is larger than the moon, slightly more than one half of the moon's spherical surface is illuminated at a given time. The boundary between the illuminated and dark regions is the **circle of illumination** (*dāʾirat al-nūr*); that separating the region visible from the observer from the hidden region is the **circle of vision** (*dāʾirat al-ruʾya*). At conjunction the two circles coincide, but the dark hemisphere faces the observer because the moon lies on the sun's side of the earth: this is **new moon** (*miḥāq*). At opposition the visible hemisphere is illuminated, producing the full moon (*badr*). At intermediate positions the two circles intersect; at quadrature at right angles, so that half of the visible lunar disk is illuminated, and otherwise at acute or obtuse angles, producing crescent and gibbous appearances. The first visible crescent after conjunction is the **hilāl**, whose emergence depends on its angular separation from the sun—given approximately as twelve degrees, though varying with the observer's location and circumstances.

The true spatial condition is a **visible conjunction**: the moon lies sufficiently near either node that its apparent latitude is less than the relevant sum of the apparent semidiameters. It then conceals some or all of the solar disk by interposing its unilluminated side, producing a partial or total eclipse. Because this is a condition relative to an observer, the event may be total for one people and partial for another, or visible to some and invisible to others, just as a hand can hide a lamp from one viewer while not hiding it from another. The limiting geometry with tangency is treated separately and does not establish an eclipse of positive magnitude.

**Lunar eclipse (*khusūf*).** At opposition, if the moon stands at or near a node so that it enters the cone of the earth's shadow, the earth intervenes between it and the sun and hides sunlight from some or all of the moon. The portion so hidden appears in its original darkness. Depending upon how much of the lunar disk is immersed in the shadow, the eclipse is total or partial. When the moon merely touches the cone's boundary there is no positive eclipsed area. This explanation depends on the geometry of opposition, inclination and shadow, not on the moon's possessing its own light.
