If the centre of a small sphere moves uniformly round a circular orbit, equal times should give equal angles at the orbital centre and equal traversed arcs; its distance from that centre should remain a radius; and a diameter through its own apex and lower point should always be aligned with that centre. In the received lunar model these three expectations do not coincide with observation. The moon's epicycle-centre appears to move uniformly with respect to the world's centre, while its apse-bearing diameter points toward a displaced point on the side of perigee, at a distance from the world-centre matching the displacement of the eccentric's centre. Al-Taftāzānī corrects a slip in *al-Mawāqif*, which instead locates it on the apogeal side. Mercury's uniformity is referred to a point halfway between the world's centre and the *mudabbir*'s centre, while Venus and the superior planets refer it to a point halfway between the world-centre and their deferent-centres. Each arrangement raises the difficulty of a motion which is uniform only around a point not straightforwardly the rotating sphere's own centre. The alignment anomaly is especially pronounced for the moon because its apse-bearing diameter does not track the centre one would expect; in the other planets alignment follows the very point relative to which the motion has been made uniform.

For Venus and Mercury a further anomaly arises from their **latitude**. Since the inclined plane crosses the representative plane, one half should lie north and the other south of the ecliptic; and because the epicycle-centre lies in the inclined plane it should sometimes traverse each half. Yet the constructed observational model keeps the centre of Venus's epicycle at a node or north of the ecliptic, and Mercury's at a node or south of it. It explains this by having the two planes alternately coincide and separate: when Venus's epicycle-centre reaches the descending node and might cross to the south, the previously northern half of the inclined plane is made southern and vice versa, so the centre remains on the northern side; Mercury behaves in the opposite fashion. But such changes of alignment require a **mover**, and the theorists have not specified one. Thus their supposedly simple, constant celestial motions have generated unexplained auxiliary requirements rather than a fully established physical astronomy.

title: Horizon, meridian, latitude and longitude; the seven climates (vol. I, pp. 346–348)
en:
**Fourth investigation: circles of positional astronomy.** The astronomers imagine further circles on the basis of observation. Their practical uses include finding the *qibla*, calculating the variation in length of day among inhabited places, and determining other astronomical quantities. The **horizon circle** separates the visible part of the celestial sphere from the concealed part. When reckoned from the centre of the earth it is the **true horizon**, a great circle; when reckoned from an observer on the earth's surface it is the **sensible horizon**, approximately a great circle, parallel to the former. Their poles are the **zenith** (*samt al-raʾs*) and **nadir** (*samt al-qadam*), the ends of the line passing through a person's upright stature and the centre of the earth, prolonged indefinitely in both directions. The sensible horizon ordinarily leaves a slightly smaller portion of the heaven visible, by a difference following the earth's radius. The distinction is perceptible with respect to the sphere of the sun and nearer objects, but the earth's radius is negligible compared with the remote spheres. Small circles parallel to the horizon above it are **almucantars of altitude** (*muqanṭarāt al-irtifāʿ*), and those below it are circles of depression.

If the horizon's poles coincide with the world's celestial poles the horizon coincides with the equator and celestial rotation resembles a millstone, as occurs where one celestial pole is overhead. If the horizon's poles differ from the world's, the horizon cuts the equator at two points, the **equinoctial east** (*maṭliʿ al-iʿtidāl*, midpoint of the eastern rising-points) and **equinoctial west** (*maghrib al-iʿtidāl*, midpoint of the western setting-points). A horizon cutting the equator at right angles is the **equatorial horizon**; otherwise it is an **oblique horizon**. There are innumerably many oblique horizons.

The **meridian circle** (*dāʾirat niṣf al-nahār*) is a great circle passing through the zenith, nadir and the two poles of the world. It receives its name because the sun's arrival at it marks the middle of the day. Al-Taftāzānī observes that this definition is not unrestricted: when the world's poles are the zenith and nadir, any circle passing through them satisfies the formula. Its poles are the eastern and western equinoctial points. It divides the equator and both the visible and hidden daily circuits into two, and permits the maximum apparent altitude of the sun and stars, when passing over it above the earth, and the maximum depth of descent when crossing beneath the earth, to be measured.

Imagine the planes of the equator, equatorial horizon and meridian extended through the whole world so that they cut the earth. Three circles result on the terrestrial surface. The **terrestrial equator**, also called the line of equinox, divides the northern and southern halves of the earth. The **equatorial horizon**, also called the horizon of the terrestrial midpoint or of the summit (*qubba*), separates the terrestrial surface facing the relevant hemisphere from that on the far side. Together these divide the earth into four quarters; the inhabited or known quarter is one of the two northern quarters, though most of its area is not actually inhabited. The third is the terrestrial **meridian**, dividing the earth into eastern and western halves.

**Latitude** (*ʿarḍ al-balad*) is the arc on a meridian between the celestial equator and a place's zenith, necessarily equal to the arc between that place's horizon and the celestial pole—its **elevation of the pole**. On the terrestrial equator the latitude is zero because the zenith lies on the celestial equator; where the horizon itself coincides with the equator the latitude reaches ninety degrees; elsewhere it measures the inclination of the horizon to the equator. Thus subtracting the sun's noon altitude on either equinox from ninety degrees gives the latitude. **Longitude** (*ṭūl al-balad*) is the arc on the equator between a given place's meridian and the meridian of the western limit of the inhabited earth. Greek astronomers measured from the west, being nearer to that end of the inhabited world; some defined it by the western ocean shore, Ptolemy by the *Eternal Isles* (*al-jazāʾir al-khālidāt*) situated farther into the sea. The competing western origins were about ten degrees apart, a distance reckoned at roughly 220 parasangs.

**Seven climates (*aqālīm*).** The geographical school held that the extreme heat near the equator and extreme cold toward the poles prevented substantial habitation there; most settled lands fell within the northern inhabited quarter, from somewhat above ten degrees to roughly fifty degrees of latitude. They divided that belt into seven regions according to differences in heat, cold and related conditions. Extent from east to west is measured by longitude; their north–south division is measured by successive differences of half an hour in the duration of the **longest day**, the day on which the sun reaches the northern solstice. Each climate lies between arcs of circles parallel to the equator, so the more northerly edge is the narrower. The first begins at latitude 12⅔°, the second at about 20° plus fractions, the third at 27½°, the fourth at about 33⅝°, the fifth near 39°, the sixth near 43⅜°, and the seventh near 47⅕°, ending just above 50°. The source reports fractional boundary values that differ slightly from modern tabulations and ought to be read as historical geodetic approximations. Some authorities instead begin the first climate at the equator and end the seventh at the furthest extent of habitation. These are conventions of regional classification, not intrinsic natural boundaries.

title: Length of day across latitudes; theological assessment of celestial astronomy (vol. I, pp. 348–349)
en:
**The equator.** Where a settlement has zero latitude the daily rotations are imagined as a **waterwheel** whose plane cuts the horizon perpendicularly. The horizon bisects each daily celestial circle; consequently day and night are essentially equal in length all year, the arc above the horizon matching the hidden arc below. A minute variation could arise from unequal secondary solar movement: if the sun moves through the apogeal half of its eccentric during the daylight it advances more slowly eastward and its apparent westward daily rotation is completed a little faster, while during a night spent in the perigeal half its eastward advance is faster and the return from west to east differs correspondingly. But the discrepancy is imperceptible. The sun reaches the zenith twice yearly, at the vernal and autumnal equinoxes; its greatest distance from the zenith comes at the two solstices. The astronomers accordingly count two summers and two winters at the equator, separated by alternating springs and autumns, and hence eight seasonal intervals of approximately a month and a half each. The apparent seasonal nomenclature describes proximity to the zenith, rather than what modern climatology would infer for every equatorial place.

**The pole.** At latitude ninety degrees the world's pole coincides with the zenith and the equator with the horizon. Celestial rotation resembles a **millstone**, and there is no unique eastern rising point, western setting point or midday meridian. Every compass direction can be a direction of rising or setting and of a body's maximum height. The celestial hemisphere adjoining the visible pole remains visible, its opposite always concealed. While the sun occupies the half of the zodiac north of the equator the pole experiences day; during its passage through the opposite half, night. The year consequently forms one continuous day and one continuous night, their durations differing slightly insofar as the sun's eastward motion is faster or slower along different parts of its course.

**Oblique horizons.** In latitudes below ninety degrees the celestial turning appears **strap-like** (*ḥamāʾilī*): the equator is inclined below the horizon toward the concealed pole, while the horizon is inclined below the equator toward the visible pole. Hence the term oblique horizon. It intersects some daily paths at angles other than right angles, touches others without crossing, and leaves some paths close to the poles wholly visible or wholly hidden. A daily circle whose distance from the relevant pole equals the latitude is tangent to the horizon; smaller circles around the visible pole never set, and corresponding circles around the invisible pole never rise. Where the horizon actually intersects a daily orbit, the visible and invisible arcs have unequal lengths; north and south of the equator the unequal portions reverse relative to northern and southern observers. Thus when the sun is in the northern zodiacal signs (Aries to Libra) day is ordinarily longer than night in northern latitudes and shorter in southern; during the southern half of the zodiac the inverse holds. The variation in night and day grows with the latitude, since the visible pole and neighbouring celestial paths ascend farther above the horizon, while the concealed pole and its paths descend farther below it. Day gains and night diminishes until the sun reaches the solstice nearer the visible pole, then the sequence reverses. For corresponding opposite zodiacal points, the daylight interval of one equals the nighttime interval of the other, as exemplified by the beginning of Cancer compared with the beginning of Capricorn.

**Concluding evaluation.** The commentator allows that much in the astronomers' description of the magnitude and striking ordering of the heavens is *possible* and supported by observational signs. Such knowledge need not contradict established religious principles; rather it can direct reflection to the divine creator. The false foundation, he argues, lies in the philosophical claim that the maker acts **by necessity** (*mūjib*), not by free choice (*mukhtār*), and in the further inference that particular celestial revolutions and configurations necessarily produce the events of the sublunary world. He calls the latter inference a root of irreligion; his objection is to assigning necessitating causal power to celestial configurations, not to using geometry to calculate them.

Some philosophers deny all colour, heat, cold, wetness and dryness to celestial bodies. They are challenged by the blue of the sky, the darkened moon at eclipse, the appearances of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, and astrological descriptions assigning Saturn coldness and dryness and Mars heat and dryness. They answer that the sky's blue is an atmospheric appearance, the eclipsed moon's blackness the absence of reflected light, planetary colours differences of luminosity, and the qualities attributed to planets and zodiacal degrees only the qualities of the effects said to appear in elemental matter when the relevant motions and configurations occur. The commentator reports these answers without accepting the alleged celestial power as established.

A second difficulty concerns **celestial simplicity**: if a sphere is utterly homogeneous, why is one part an equator, another a pole, another the mounting-place of a star, and another the site of an epicycle? title: The four simple elements and their role in compounded bodies (vol. I, pp. 350–351)
en:
**Second subdivision: simple elemental bodies (*al-basāʾiṭ al-ʿunṣuriyya*).** The predominating philosophical account posits **four elements**, fire, air, water and earth. Sensory and experimental evidence, together with consideration of composition and resolution, suggests that elemental substances, whether simple or compounded, exhibit four fundamental tactile qualities: hot, cold, moist and dry. No simple element has been observed possessing only one of them, and three or four cannot be present simultaneously, because hot is contrary to cold and moist to dry. Consequently each element must combine one member from each contrary pair: **fire** hot and dry; **air** hot and moist; **water** cold and moist; **earth** cold and dry.

Several attempted rational divisions support this count. One begins with the alternative hot/cold and subdivides each by dry/moist. Another begins with heavy/light and subdivides each into absolute and relative kinds. Another asks whether the component is subtle or dense: the subtle that burns what it meets is fire, the subtle that does not is air; the dense that flows is water, the dense that does not is earth. Yet another distinguishes easy or difficult reception of shapes and whether parts cohere or separate. The commentator insists that the real support is **inductive observation**, not these abstract divisions. Al-Rāzī, recounting Avicenna's lengthy analysis and objections in the *Mabāḥith*, concludes that whoever seeks a demonstratively exhaustive enumeration of the elements by a merely rational division undertakes what he cannot accomplish. Investigators found, through combining and decomposing bodies, that many things arose from four kinds and could be reduced to them, while the four did not visibly resolve into yet more elementary bodies; on this empirical basis they called them elements (*ustuqussāt*).

Older alternatives proposed one fundamental element—fire, air, water, earth or vapour—from which the others arise by transformation; others proposed two, such as fire and earth, water and earth, or air and earth; still others proposed three, excluding water as condensed air or excluding fire as intensely heated air. None, says the text, introduced a doubt sufficient to refute the induction favouring four. But **three uncertainties remain serious**. First, the existence of a distinct *sphere of fire* has not been established. Meteors do not prove its existence, since the luminous phenomena could be caused otherwise, especially in the theologians' framework; the visible flame may be intensely heated air rather than a separate substance. Second, the **dryness of pure fire**, in the technical sense of resistance to taking and losing shapes, cannot be observed or experimentally tested in a hypothetical pure sphere surrounding the air; earthly flame mixed with other matter rather suggests the contrary. A proof from the fact that extreme heat destroys moisture is insufficient, because it may destroy wet material and watery constituents without eliminating the specific physical disposition called *moistness*—air is a possible counterexample. Third, the **heat of unmixed air** is also not independently proved. Observations find increasingly cold air at higher elevations, up to bitter frost. The claim that this is only because of proximity to cold earth and water and the absence of reflected sunlight requires further demonstration. Arguments that fire must be dry lest it be air, or air hot lest it be water, are circularly dependent on their proposed elemental definitions; shared effects or graded properties do not establish identity of underlying essence.

**The three classes of generated compounds.** Philosophers call the four the constitutive principles of sublunary composites (*mawālīd*), grouped as minerals, plants and animals. They argue from **composition**: earth mingled with water and interspersed air, acted upon by heat from the sun, produces vegetation; vegetation in turn becomes nourishment and, after transformations, part of animal bodies. Without moisture, interpenetrating air or a cooking heat, the observed composite would not form. They argue from **analysis**: when a compounded body is placed in a distilling vessel (*qarʿ wa-anbīq*) and heated, airy constituents rise, liquid portions condense and flow down, and earthy material remains. Fire is inferred as the necessary source of the cooking and maturation which produce a mixed **temperament** (*mizāj*) and hence prepare for a *specific form* (*ṣūra nawʿiyya*) preserving the aggregate from dissolution when its external causes have passed away.

Two doubts are addressed. Heat generally separates unlike substances: how then can it keep them together? The reply distinguishes heat's preparatory role in producing the mixed temperament from the subsequent specific form which preserves the parts. Could continuing proximity of the parts, rather than a specific form, explain their coherence? Such continuing causes may themselves pass away; but the objection points to a real alternative. More decisive remaining criticisms ask why the required cooking could not proceed from the heat of airy parts or radiation from celestial bodies without a **fiery part** and why an aggregate could not be preserved simply by the will of a freely choosing Creator or by the intermixture of moist and dry components. Even if fourfold analysis is correct for observed specimens, it does not establish that **every** compound must have the same composition. The generalization outruns the experiment.

title: Conversion of the elements and the disputed formation of dew (vol. I, pp. 351–352)
en:
**Second investigation: elemental conversion (*istihāla*).** Philosophers hold the four elements to have a common **prime matter** (*hayūlā*) capable of receiving their distinct substantial forms. The particular form actualized depends on dispositions established by external causes. When those causes and dispositions change, one form may vanish—**corruption** (*fasād*)—and a new form arise—**generation** (*kawn*). In this sense, and not by the persistence of one and the same completed specific form, one element turns into another.

Their order is fire outermost, then air, water and earth. Any of the four can transform into an adjacent element: fire/air, air/water, or water/earth. A transformation between nonadjacent elements may require one intermediate element, as fire/water or air/earth, or two intermediates, as fire/earth. Each pairing permits transformation in both directions, yielding six direct kinds, four kinds through one intermediary and two through two: twelve ordered forms of elemental conversion, namely four starting elements each convertible into the remaining three. Sensory observation and experiment are invoked for all the cases.

One case is particularly disputed, **air into water**. Moisture accumulating on the outside of a vessel cooled with ice might come from liquid **seeping** through its wall, or from airborne particles of water already suspended nearby being drawn together and deposited. Abū al-Barakāt explains the second possibility: exceedingly small watery particles are dispersed in the surrounding air but remain aloft while heat keeps them tenuous; cooling near the ice-cold vessel causes them to thicken, grow heavier, descend and gather as droplets. Against seepage the reply says that hot water, being thinner, should pass through even more readily, and seepage could explain at most particular seams, not moisture appearing all round the vessel, especially not a vessel merely inverted over ice. Against deposition from pre-existing airborne water, the text argues that water particles in hot summer air should evaporate and rise, and that a limited local supply should soon be exhausted after repeatedly wiping the moisture away. A supply from increasingly distant air should take progressively longer, contrary to the apparent observation; and particles descending in straight lines would not explain why droplets collect on the vessel's vertical sides. These replies are given as arguments of the historical debate rather than as modern thermodynamics. The deeper point remains that what we observe is condensation or deposition; the philosophical inference to a substantial conversion of *air itself* into *water itself* requires the explanatory framework being disputed.

title: The layers of fire, air, water and earth; their natural arrangement (vol. I, pp. 352–354)
en:
**Third investigation: disposition of the elementary regions.** Because fire is thought intensely to convert neighbouring things into its own substance through the strength of its heat, it was assigned **one single layer**, with both convex and concave surfaces spherical as befits a simple element left undisturbed in its natural state. The exception is among those who regard fire not as a separate element but as air heated by the celestial sphere's motion; on their premise the slow rotation nearer the pole and faster motion nearer the celestial equator produce different amounts of heat and expansion, so the inner surface of the fiery region will not be a perfect sphere. The rotation of an enclosing body does not by itself entail rotation of the enclosed body even where centres coincide, though auxiliary causes might carry the latter along. Astronomers cite the movement of meteors and tailed stars with the heavens as evidence for a fiery sphere moving with its container. They say the air does not follow because its moisture makes its constituents readily change places and so lose their adhesion to the enclosing body. Some assert that every part of fire has a determinate adjoining part of the heaven as a natural place and follows that part in rotation. The reply denies that a homogeneous fire can naturally single out one part of a homogeneous celestial sphere rather than another: the proposed natural attachment has no ground in their own principle of homogeneity.

**Air** is regarded, in the preferable philosophical account, as spherical on its upper convex boundary, where it touches the concave fiery boundary, but irregular on its inner surface, given mountains, valleys and waters. Four atmospheric levels are specified. First is the **smoky layer** adjoining fire, permeated by fiery particles and by smoke rising from below, thus mixing earthly, airy and fiery constituents. Beneath it lies a **purer layer**, reached by smoke but not by vapour: smoke is deemed subtler and lighter owing to its fiery admixture and its rising from a dry source, whereas vapour is less penetrating. Next is the intensely cold **frost-bearing layer** (*al-ṭabaqa al-zamharīriyya*), where the ascending vapours are no longer warmed by the reflection of rays from the stars. Lowest is the layer neighbouring the earth, heated by light reflected from the surface on which the rays fall. **Water** forms a single encompassing layer of seas around the earth, although its full purity is lost through solar effects and the mingling of earthy particles. Differences in sweetness, salinity, clarity and turbidity are ascribed to different degrees of that admixture. **Earth** has three levels: a hard outer region partly exposed above water and dried by sunlight, partly submerged; a muddy intermediate mixture of earth and water; and the pure earthy layer near the centre. Thus these conventional divisions count **nine elemental layers**. The author of *al-Mawāqif* counted seven by excluding water as a distinct surrounding spherical layer and allotting air only three, with the upper level an airy-fiery mixture, the middle “frosty” pure air and the lower a watery-airy vapour. Al-Taftāzānī challenges that assignment: why should a layer distant from water and earth be identified with the coldest region, and why should the frost-bearing layer be supposed to be unmixed air?

**Earth and water together.** These are treated as composing a sphere whose centre is the world's centre. The earth is not strictly spherical, owing to mountains and depressions. Saying that its inequalities do not undermine its sphericity means only that, at the scale of the whole body, the deviations are too small to be perceptible. One old geometer compares the height of the highest mountain, reckoned at roughly two and one-third parasangs, with scarcely a fraction of a barley-grain's breadth on a globe one cubit across. Yet exact sphericity is an absolute geometrical predicate: **all radii must be equal**, and any variation, however small, destroys exact equality. It is improper to treat exact sphericity itself as admitting degrees.

On the philosophers' principles water, as relatively heavy, should occupy its natural sphere above absolutely heavy earth and beneath air, wholly surrounding the earth. How, then, is an inhabited terrestrial quarter exposed? One explanation says solar heat draws a greater mass of water southward, since the sun's perigee lies in southern zodiacal signs and its apogee in northern signs, making its rays stronger to the south. The sun's apogee would then shift through time, moving the inhabited region between hemispheres, so that habitation lies where the sun is further away, avoiding catastrophic summer heat and extreme winter cold. Another explanation posits more low-lying basins in the north owing to accidental external causes: water naturally flows into them and leaves elevated parts exposed. Others can offer no known natural cause and appeal to **eternal providence** (*ʿināya azalīya*). If providence means that God **willed** the appearance of a stable abode for humans and animals, with minerals and plants sufficient for their livelihood, they have approached the truth by recognising a maker who knows particulars and acts by choice. But if they understand providence only as eternal knowledge of the most perfect total order, it does not, on their principles, establish divine knowledge of particular things *as particulars* or purposive choice.

**The centre and supposed immobility of the earth.** The natural philosophers and geometers concur, within this historical model, that the elements are approximately spherical and that earth lies centrally, like the centre of the sphere to its circumference, neither moving to the centre, away from it, nor rotating upon it. Geometrical arguments in astronomy are said to establish the facts (*anniyya*), while natural-philosophical arguments purport to establish why they must be so (*limmiyya*). A simple nature allegedly has a spherical natural shape because one nature acts similarly in every direction. Earth is absolutely heavy and tends toward the world's centre, the lowest place as determined by the outer celestial sphere; settled in its natural location, it cannot move away or further inward. The straight inclination (*mayl mustaqīm*) evident in its parts is said to exclude a contrary circular inclination (*mayl mustadīr*); this is directed against those who explain daily rising and setting through the earth's **west-to-east rotation upon its axis**. Al-Taftāzānī finds these physical demonstrations weak. They prove at best an inherent tendency, not that the earth must remain so **in actual existence**: a coercing agent might alter its shape, move it away from the centre, or produce circular movement without circular movement being natural to it. Here he treats the geographical arrangement as an account of observational astronomy but refuses to infer its absolute natural necessity. Among geometrical arguments for the sea's curvature, an approaching vessel sees the **top of a high coastal mountain before its lower parts**; placing fires at different heights makes the sequence observable. The other astronomical proofs and their objections are reviewed in the continuation.

title: Evidence for the earth's curvature; vapours, clouds, precipitation, thunder, lightning and winds (vol. I, pp. 355–357)
en:
**Further geometrical considerations about the earth.** If the earth did not occupy a central position, say the astronomers, a fixed star would appear much smaller to observers at some terrestrial locations because of their greater separation from it and larger to others because of their nearness; this is not what is observed. If its surface were flat from east to west, the times of rising and setting of the same stars would agree for people at the same latitude; if it were concave, those farther west would see them earlier. Instead, eastern observers encounter celestial risings and settings before western observers. This is tested with **lunar eclipses**, whose middle necessarily occurs at one instant for all observers, although the local hours counted since nightfall differ. When one place records the eclipse two hours into night, a place farther east might record it three hours into night, if their meridians are separated by fifteen degrees and the corresponding land distance is calculated at about a thousand miles. The observed pattern supports **east–west convexity**.

A flat north–south extension would preserve the visible pole's altitude no matter how far an observer travelled; a concave one would yield the reverse of the observed trend. In fact the northern pole rises as one travels northward, the southern one as one travels southward, while the opposite pole descends. Hence **north–south convexity**, and corresponding curvature in intermediate directions where the effects are compounded. Having established curvature for the exposed portion, they infer that the unexposed surface is similar. The objection is again logical: other causes might conceivably produce the recorded appearances, so from an observed effect one cannot infer a *unique* cause unless alternatives are excluded. Moreover, even if the argument succeeds, the observations prove at most centrality and roundness **to the senses**, not mathematically exact roundness or centrality. The astronomer must admit a judgement of the kind called *ḥads*, as with the inference that moonlight is received from the sun.

**Third subdivision: weakly mixed compounds, without a true temperament.** After the celestial and elemental simple bodies, the treatise examines composites whose mixture has not reached the complete integration called *mizāj*. These are nearer to the simples: some can comprise only two or three elements. They are divided by region of generation: things produced **above** the earth in the air, **on** the earth's surface, and **within** the earth. Atmospheric effects arise chiefly from **vapour** (*bukhār*) and **smoke** (*dukhān*), both of which heat releases. From moist material heat separates airy and watery particles, producing vapour; from dry material it lifts earthly particles mingled with fiery and often airy particles, producing smoke.

Rising vapour may be so attenuated by heat that its watery constituents become air. Or it may reach the frost-bearing atmospheric layer, thicken into a cloud, and descend as **rain** if the cold is moderate. If strong cold freezes the cloud before drops have formed, it falls as **snow**; if freezing follows the formation of droplets, it falls as **hail**. Small, rounded hail may come from more distant clouds, its corners worn away by movement and friction; otherwise hailstones tend to be larger and irregular. Hail is expected chiefly in transitional spring or autumn weather, since strong summer rarefaction and winter freezing do not favour the same sequence. Vapour which does not reach the frost-bearing layer can remain near earth as **fog**, if plentiful; if less plentiful and condensed by the cool night, it forms **frost** upon freezing or **dew** if still liquid. Thus frost is to dew as snow is to rain. Dense rain clouds can also form from ample vapour cooled before reaching the supposed upper frost zone, because obstructing winds or a mountain-facing wind presses the vapour together, or because heavy, slower portions prevent the whole mass from rising further.

Sometimes smoke accompanies rising vapour. On entering colder air the vapour forms a cloud enclosing smoke. Smoke remaining hot tends to ascend; if cooled, it tends to descend. Either movement may violently rupture the cloud and, through rupture and impact, produce the sound of **thunder**. A thin fiery appearance is **lightning**, while a thicker fiery manifestation is the **thunderbolt** (*ṣāʿiqa*). Thick smoke, on reaching the supposed sphere of fire, might ignite as smoke from an extinguished lamp can catch fire from a still-lit one; to a distant observer the flame appears as a **falling star or meteor** (*shihāb*). If thick smoke burns without igniting in that way, its sustained glowing can be imagined as a tuft, tail, serpent, or horned beast—historical interpretations of comets and other luminous appearances. It may stand beneath a planet or circulate with fire as fire follows the celestial sphere. Dark and red portentous appearances are ascribed to denser smoke. If a continuous column of smoke reaches the earth while its burning front moves downward, it can look like a fiery dragon descending from heaven, called a *ḥarīq*. These accounts are historical theories, not modern explanations of the phenomena.

**Winds and vortices.** When much smoke rises and is cooled in the frost-bearing layer, its heat is broken, it gains weight and descends, setting air into waves and producing a **cold wind**. If its heat remains, the smoke approaches the region of fire and later returns with motion imparted by the moving heaven, producing a **hot wind**. The author's gloss on *al-Mawāqif* clarifies that the smoke need only reach the proximity of the fiery sphere and take motion from it; it cannot literally traverse the transforming fire, laden with heavy earthy parts, to strike the heavenly body itself. An alternative cause of wind is **rarefaction** on one side of a mass of air, displacing adjoining air and propagating the movement. In general **wind is air in movement**, regardless of the particular trigger. A rising circular whirlwind may result from opposing winds meeting. A descending vortex may arise when wind released from a cloud falls against an ascending cloud or current, so that part of the air is squeezed between pressures above and below, whirls, and presses down earthy particles in a twisting path. The text then qualifies these constructions by appealing to the actual extraordinary force of winds, capable of uprooting trees and snatching ships from the sea; the critique continues in the following passage.

title: Halos, rainbows and a witnessed lunar rainbow; mountains and earthquakes (vol. I, pp. 357–358)
en:
The extraordinary power of winds—uprooting trees, seizing ships, and, according to well-attested accounts, devastating whole towns—together with scriptural evidence, should turn the investigator back to **the freely choosing omnipotent agent**. At most, the physical explanations just rehearsed identify possible **material causes** of the phenomena. They do not remove their dependence on the Creator.

**Halos (*hāla*) and the rainbow (*qaws quzaḥ*).** A halo around the moon is explained by tiny, smooth, dewy particles clustered like mirrors in a thin, transparent cloud opposite the moon. The moon itself is seen directly through the cloud, but its image or light is reflected by the many minute polished droplets. Because a tiny mirror reproduces the object's brightness and perhaps colour rather than its complete shape, each droplet conveys a luminous appearance. Droplets disposed at the same angular relation to the moon collectively display a bright circle. The thin cloud is invisible under stronger moonlight, just as floating dust is imperceptible in a brightly illuminated desert. Halos most often appear in calm conditions. Their breaking apart in all directions is taken as a sign of clearing, a breach in one direction as a sign of wind approaching from that side, and disappearance owing to thickening clouds as a sign of rain. Two thin clouds at different heights may produce doubled halos, the lower and nearer one appearing larger; some report seven at once. A solar halo, also called *ṭafāwa*, is thought much rarer, because strong sunshine disperses the delicate cloud needed for the appearance.

The **rainbow** is explained by transparent, clear watery droplets lying away from the sun, with a dense dark backdrop such as a mountain or cloud, as coloured objects placed behind a crystalline substance make the reflected light visible. When the sun is near the horizon and an observer faces the droplets, each tiny polished droplet reflects sunlight but not the sun's full circular form, producing a curved luminous band. Its apparent geometry is that of a circle centred on the direction opposite the sun, whose lower part lies below the horizon; as the sun rises the visible arc becomes smaller, disappearing when the sun is high overhead. One proposed explanation of its colours makes the upper part, being closer to the sun, strongly red, and the lower part more darkly purplish because its illumination is weaker, with an intermediate shade between them. The commentator objects that this gives merely a continuous gradation from bright red to purple, not the distinct bands observed; also the proposed intermediate shade does not derive naturally from the alleged mixture of colours. **Avicenna himself acknowledged that the cause of these colour differences was not known to him**.

**Al-Taftāzānī's observation.** Though astronomers say the moon rarely makes a faint, colourless bow, he reports: “I myself saw, in Turkistan in the year 763 [AH], on the side opposite the moon, a bow having the colours of a rainbow. It was far smaller and nearly a full circle; its colours were less pure and luminous than those made by the sun, being denser. The night was damp, with thin clouds, and the moon stood near the horizon.” This is the author's first-person observation and should not be silently converted into an anonymous generalization. Its occurrence directly qualifies the alleged rule that a lunar bow has no colours.

**Second kind: things formed on the earth's surface.** Examples are stones and mountains. Earth ordinarily hardens into stone when heat acts upon sticky mud and binds its moisture to its dry particles. Flowing water can also solidify as stone through a mineral petrifying virtue, or because its earthy principle predominates **in power**, even where not predominating in bulk, as in salt. Large masses of viscous mud exposed to great heat, suddenly or over time, can harden into great rocks. Such a rock becomes a mountain if an earthquake raises land into a hill, or if piled ruins later solidify, or if its material differs in hardness so that winds and waters remove the softer portions and leave resistant portions standing high, or through other causes. Many mountains show successive strata like courses of masonry. This suggests that the lower layer hardened before the upper was laid down, with dissimilar material deposited between them. Aquatic animal remains are found enclosed in broken rocks; from this one may infer that lands now inhabited were formerly submerged beneath the sea, where extensive muddy deposits hardened after exposure, with streams and winds cutting valleys between the resulting heights. Mountains are also said to retain ascending vapours, making them the source-material for mineral deposits, clouds and springs; in loose and porous ground the vapours escape too readily to collect in quantity.

**Third kind: phenomena formed within the earth.** An **earthquake** occurs when something below the surface moves and moves the earth lying above it. Vapour, smoke, wind or a similar force may build within cavities beneath a dense surface whose passages are blocked or very narrow. In struggling to escape it shakes or ruptures the earth, sometimes with fire and fearful sounds produced by grinding and impact; roaring noises may come from the strong winds within. Earthquakes are said to be infrequent in loose soils that let vapour escape, and less common in summer because the surface is less closed. The author reports a practical inference that numerous deep wells can create exits for trapped vapours and reduce earthquakes. Sudden cooling during an eclipse is also proposed as a cause: the sun's rays are briefly removed, the cold rapidly contracts the enclosed gases, and their action differs from the more gradual effects of ordinary cooling. These are records of historical natural theory, not confirmed modern causal explanations. The discussion proceeds to springs, wells and subterranean water.

title: Underground water, the limits of natural explanation, and accounts of extraordinary effects (I.359–360)
en:
**The formation of springs and wells.** If the vapours produced underground are abundant and turn into water, the earth is split open by them. If a continuing supply feeds them, running springs result. Their uninterrupted flow is explained, on the philosophers' account, by the necessity of avoiding a void: whenever the water flows out, air or further vapour is drawn into its place, becomes chilled by the cold there, and is likewise converted into water. This continues unless something intervenes to prevent it, whether all at once or by degrees. When no additional supply feeds the vapours, standing springs result. If the vapours are not abundant enough to split the earth, then, when the weight of the overlying soil is removed and they find a passage, they are discharged through it. Flowing channels or wells then result, according as the supply continues or fails. Rainwater and melted snow can also account for springs, channels and wells, for we observe their waters to increase when rainfall and snow increase and to diminish when these diminish.

**The degree of certainty available to such explanations.** When the author says, “Then they themselves acknowledge,” he is indicating that these accounts of upper effects—those above the surface of the earth—and lower effects—those upon and beneath its surface—are the views of the philosophers, not of the theologians, who refer all such occurrences to the will of the powerful, freely choosing Agent. Yet the philosophers themselves acknowledge that the accounts are *conjectures* based on intellectual surmise (*ḥads*) and experience. We observe things analogous to them: in a bathhouse, vapours rise, thicken, and drip; in severe cold what issues from the breath becomes dense like snow; and in mirrors images and colours vary while lights are reflected in diverse ways. Such observations and experiences, and others like them, give grounds for supposing that the reported effects proceed from the causes assigned to them.

Other circumstantial indications may accompany these observations and yield *intuitive certainty* (*yaqīn ḥadsī*). This varies with the person: one observer attains certainty while another does not. The philosophers also admit that these effects might derive from **other causes**, since something of one and the same species can have several causes, and its production from some of them may be rare whereas from others it is frequent. They further admit that several of the causes they enumerate are judged by surmise **not to constitute sufficient causes by themselves**. Such causes require the addition of spiritual powers, without which they would not suffice to necessitate the effects attributed to them.

**Examples cited against an exhaustive material explanation.** Some winds uproot great trees and seize ships from the seas. Some thunderbolts strike a mountain and shatter it, or strike the sea and plunge into it, burning certain of its animals. Some pass through something porous without burning it, yet liquefy the dense, hard bodies they encounter: they melt gold inside a purse without burning the purse, apart from whatever is scorched by the melting; or they melt the metal boss of a shield without burning the shield. Some comets remain for several months and display movements both in longitude and in latitude. There are other strange occurrences of the same sort, for which, the philosophers acknowledge, the material and efficient causes previously listed do not suffice. They accordingly posit an operation of spiritual powers.

Reports from the lands of the Turks and from the districts of Aras and Bulghār concerning the distinctive powers of plants and stones, and concerning clouds, winds and rain, have, he says, been so widely transmitted that the mind judges the effects not to proceed simply from plant or stone, but from the Creator of powers and capacities. He adds a report in the first person: “I have heard from more than one trustworthy person” that, when travelling during the summer, some people take along one of the unbelievers who knows how to use certain stones. While using them, he entreats and supplicates the Creator—glory be to Him—according to his people's manner of worship. He practices severe ascetic discipline, refrains from desires, and belongs to a particular group widely known for bringing down rain. Thereupon a cloud is produced, large enough to shade the travellers, and a wind that protects them from mosquitoes. The cloud and wind move when they move, stop when they stop, and turn back when they turn back. Sometimes another group approaches, accompanied by its own sufficient cloud and a wind blowing contrary to the first. To deny such occurrences, in the estimation of the people concerned, is like denying what is manifest to the senses.

The account of a plant which, when brought into contact with an iron fetter fastened to a horse's legs, causes it to open is likewise well known, he says. “By my life,” he concludes, the transmitted texts which ascribe such effects to the powerful, freely choosing Agent are decisive, and the paths of guidance to that conclusion are clear. But **“one to whom God grants no light has no light”** (cf. Qurʾān 24:40).

**Editorial note.** The contrast between experimental conjecture, individual *ḥads*, and theological attribution is part of the argument; the commentator is *reporting* the unusual phenomena, not providing an independently verified account of them. The geographical form «أرس» is retained provisionally as *Aras*, pending examination of the printed witness.

title: The fourth subdivision of bodies: definition and derivation of temperament
en:
The fourth subdivision now begins. It is the fourth of the subdivisions into which the detailed investigation of bodies was arranged, and it concerns composites possessing a *temperament* (*mizāj*). Its introduction explains what temperament is and how it is divided; three investigations then concern the three kinds of composite, namely minerals, plants, and animals. It has already been explained that the treatment of these matters follows the principles accepted in philosophy.

In explaining temperament, the author chose a procedure of unfolding the account (*tafrīʿ*) rather than giving the definition at once. He could instead have said: "It is an intermediate, homogeneous quality, arising from the mutual interaction of elements whose parts have been made small and brought together, through their powers, with the intensity of each of their four qualities being broken down." title: First clarification: minute elemental parts and bodily contact
en:
**First.** Smallness of the elemental parts is included in the account of temperament. A body can produce an effect without contact—as the sun heats the earth, or a magnet attracts iron—but in the production of a mixture the interaction takes place by contact. Contact increases as the surfaces increase; surfaces multiply when the parts are multiplied; and the parts multiply when they become smaller. Thus the finer the elemental subdivision, the more complete the mixture.

Some make contact a condition of every bodily action. If no positional relation at all were required, that would be plainly false: a fire in the Ḥijāz does not burn wood in Iraq. If, on the other hand, they require proximity, even across one or more intermediaries, a remote receptive body is affected only after the nearer body capable of receiving the influence has been affected. Consequently, they say, the intermediate body, acting through the influence it has acquired, is what acts upon the remote body: an object beside air adjoining a fire is heated by the heating of the air. There would, on this argument, be no bodily action without contact. The answer is that the remote body may be receptive while the intervening body is not, so that an action without contact is possible, as illustrated by the sun's heating the earth and the magnet's attraction of iron.

title: Second clarification: must all four elements enter a temperament?
en: **Second.** One position holds that all four elements are necessary for the production of a temperament: each contributes something without which the mutual breaking of intensities and the production of a homogeneous intermediate quality are incomplete. On this view obtaining the fiery component requires generation and corruption (*kawn wa-fasād*), since fire does not descend from the ethereal region except under compulsion, and no such compelling agency is present. Others allow a temperament to arise from the union of only some of the elements: if their parts become sufficiently minute and intermingled, they inevitably interact and an intermediate quality results.

title: Third clarification: do qualities or substantial forms act?
en:
**Third.** In the physician's account, when the elements combine, the acting and acted-upon factors are the four qualities, because the physician does not establish a specific substantial form (*ṣūra nawʿiyya*) in the way the philosophers do. Philosophers who affirm those forms on the arguments previously given make the form the agent, acting through a quality belonging to its matter either essentially (such as fire's heat) or accidentally (such as heat acquired by water). The form's agency means that it brings the matter of the other element toward its own quality, breaking the *intensity* (*sawra*) of the other's quality: that degree of the quality passes away and another, weaker degree arises.

Why is form made the agent? It cannot be matter, whose function is receptivity and being affected. Nor, they argue, can it be the quality itself. For if the two opposed qualities were simultaneously to break one another's intensity, the same thing would be overcome by another at the very instant that it overcame the other. If this happened successively—one first diminished the other and was then diminished by it—the defeated would become victorious over its conqueror, and the victor would become defeated. The very quality which had failed to overcome its opposite when it was strong would, after weakening, succeed in overcoming it; this is impossible. Yet the quality must mediate the process, because it is opposition that accounts for breaking and being broken, and opposition is found in qualities. Thus the cold aerial form does not destroy the coldness of earth, nor the form of heated water the heat of air, and so forth.

The objection is that this difficulty applies equally to the philosophers' own view. If two forms act through their qualities simultaneously, the same victory and defeat must coexist: a quality remains victorious even when its role is only to mediate the victory of the form. Moreover, the intense quality through which the reduction is caused and the weaker quality produced by it would have to coexist at one instant, although these are different degrees. If the process is successive, the same inversion of victor and defeated follows. Because the objection is clear, and because effect must coincide with its cause and conditions, *al-Mawāqif* confines its formulation to the simultaneous alternative: the form can act only through the quality, so that the quality is a condition of efficacy; but then the breaking quality and the newly produced, weaker quality would coexist.

It might be proposed to escape the objection in two ways. First, speaking of the form's agency could be figurative. Strictly, forms and qualities are merely preparatory causes disposing matter for the effusion of an intermediate quality from a separate principle. Philosophers explain this effusion as necessary once the complete agent and receptive subject are present, while others explain it according to divine custom because the agent chooses freely. On this construal the whole language of victory and defeat is set aside. Second, what is overcome in mixing may be the *intensity* of each quality, while what overcomes it is the opposite quality itself—not its intensity. This is manifest in the case of extremely hot water being cooled not only by extremely cold water but by tepid water, or even by water that is hot yet less hot. Accordingly a quality whose own intensity is being reduced may nevertheless reduce the intensity of its opposite; this is not one and the same thing's simultaneously being victor and defeated.

The reply is that, if these answers are accepted, one may equally say that the qualities interact without invoking specific forms at all. There is a further objection: we observe an intermediate quality produced through the interaction of qualities without finding a separate form that reduces the other's intensity—for example, when hot and cold water are mixed. The water-form certainly does not, as water-form, break coldness. If the philosophers say that no proper action and passion occurs here, and that the two bodies of water simply dispose matter to lose their earlier qualities and to receive an intermediate one from the overflowing principle, we answer: let exactly that be true of temperament. A quality's becoming more or less intense means that a quality ceases and another, more or less intense, arises according to changed receptivity. The question in dispute is only what is the agent.

If they instead say that the fire-form responsible for heating the hot water is what breaks the coldness of the other water, they have conceded that the form acting on a quality need not be the form of one of the simple elemental parts of the resulting compound. This overturns their claim that qualities are broken in temperament exclusively by the forms of the combining elements.

The more plausible philosophical account would make the *water-form* of the hot water act through its acquired, accidental heat upon the cold water's coldness. It is one of their principles that the form of each element acts directly upon its own matter and upon a neighbouring matter through a quality, whether that quality is essential (water's coldness) or accidental (water's acquired heat), active (heat and cold) or passive (moisture and dryness). An element's matter likewise receives influence from its own form and intrinsic or acquired qualities, and from what adjoins it. This formulation avoids objections levelled at qualities as agents: that an active quality would have to undergo passion when heat and cold oppose one another, or that a passive quality would have to exercise agency when moisture and dryness oppose one another.

If it is said that, however obscure the agent may be, what receives the effect in mixing is clearly the qualities—fire's heat, water's coldness, and the rest—we answer: yes, in the sense that those qualities cease and an intermediate quality comes to be. But the underlying thing which is actually affected and changes from one condition to another is **matter** alone. Just as matter may be affected in respect of active qualities such as heat and cold, so a form may act by means of passive qualities such as moisture and dryness. It is evident, on this doctrine, that water's form breaks fire's dryness through water's moisture, not through its coldness; and fire's form breaks water's moisture through fire's dryness, not through its heat.

title: Fourth clarification: homogeneity throughout the mixture
en:
**Fourth.** For the temperament-quality to be "homogeneous throughout" means that what is present in each part of the composite, whether the part itself is compounded or simple, is of the *same species* as what is present in every other part: the only difference is its subject. Thus its fiery and watery portions are alike as regards heat, cold, moisture and dryness, as are its airy and earthy portions.

Suppose instead that different elemental qualities remained unchanged in the several parts, but were so closely mixed that the senses could not discriminate them, producing only the *appearance* of homogeneity. There would have been no genuine mutual action and affection, nor would there exist a really unified qualitative condition disposing the composite to receive a mineral, vegetable, or animal form, or a human soul. There would be only the aggregation and juxtaposition of elements. True *imtizāj* is their combination in such a way that a uniform intermediate quality comes to be. *Tarkīb* (composition) is broader than this, as is *ikhtilāṭ* (mingling), although *al-Shifāʾ* also uses the latter as synonymous with mixing in this stricter sense.

A commentator on the *Canon* suggests that homogeneity in all parts merely means that a mixture feels hot relative to something colder and cold relative to something hotter, and so likewise for wet and dry. This was intended to answer the Imām's objection that concomitants of temperament would otherwise fall within the definition. But it conflicts with what reason and reliable textual transmission expressly establish. The explanation given here is what the expression naturally means and what is stated in the philosophers' own accounts.

title: The necessity of qualitative alteration (istihala)
en:
**Authorial lemma: "The elements must therefore undergo alteration in all their qualities."** We have already distinguished *generation and corruption* (*kawn wa-fasād*), in which one specific substantial form ceases and another arises while matter remains, from *alteration* (*istiḥāla*), in which a quality ceases and another arises while the form remains. Clearly the view of temperament just expounded—an intermediate homogeneous quality really present in every part—depends upon allowing each element to undergo alteration in its active and passive qualities. A fiery part of the mixture must then share the same intermediate condition in heat, cold, wetness and dryness as the watery, airy and earthy parts.

The Imām [al-Rāzī] claimed that philosophers had established this only for water, whose coldness can change into heat without the production or appearance of another substantial thing, nor the arrival of something from outside. That does not establish every element's capacity to change in every such quality. Physicians, he alleged, handed the explanation of this principle to philosophers as a foundational principle of medicine, while philosophers handed it to physicians as a derivative question of natural philosophy and a foundation of medicine. It therefore remained uninvestigated.

The reply is that the possibility of alteration follows from the possibility of generation and corruption. Establishing the latter in the elements therefore also establishes the former. As indicated in the *Najāt*, the loss of one form and arrival of another happens only when matter's preparedness is complete. Preparedness is itself something originated, requiring time; hence some change must occur gradually. That gradual change cannot belong to the substantial form itself, whose existence or nonexistence is instantaneous. It must therefore belong to quality: the quality appropriate to the disappearing form weakens, while that appropriate to the emerging form strengthens. Alteration means precisely this change of quality while the form remains.

The concise text proposes another proof: since the effusion of substantial forms and souls has been established, there must first arise in every portion of the compound a homogeneous intermediate quality preparing its matter to receive them. That is just the alteration of the elemental parts from their unmixed qualities to the new intermediate quality. **But this proof is open to objection**: the necessary preparedness might be produced by the mere intermingling of minutely divided parts, yielding a quality intermediate *to the senses*, while each simple elemental part retains its unmixed quality.

title: Primary and secondary temperament
en:
**Authorial lemma: "The definition also covers secondary temperament."** This is the temperament resulting from the mingling of minute parts of *compounded* bodies, as the temperament of gold is supposed to arise from mercury and sulphur. It falls under the definition if we take its production to be a breaking of intensities by means of simple elemental forms preserved in the mixture, as seems apparent from distillation and alembic experiments. For example, a piece of flesh placed in such apparatus separates into a watery, dripping component and an earthy, calcined one.

But suppose a different account: the elemental combination first disposes the parts for the effusion of a *new specific form* other than the elemental forms. The resulting composites then interact by means of their own specific forms and qualities, producing a homogeneous intermediate quality in the whole—as in gold through the forms of mercury and sulphur. Such a **secondary temperament** would not be included in the earlier definition, for it would not have arisen from the interaction of the elements by their powers, that is, by their elemental forms or qualities.

title: The Peripatetic view and two rejected alternatives
en:
**Authorial lemma: "Temperament is therefore another species [of quality]."** It is apparent from the preceding discussion that temperament is a tangible quality specifically different from the unmixed qualities of the elements. It exists in each of the mixed parts, including the simple elemental parts: their specific forms persist, but their original, unmixed qualities have undergone alteration into the intermediate one. This is the position of the majority of the Peripatetics.

Objection: if the elemental forms remain and the new form generated after mixing pervades all portions, then, for example, fire would bear both the fiery form and the golden form; and it would follow that natural compounds could be generated from a single element. Reply: the new form may extend only through the compound portions and not the simple ones; or a simple portion's reception of that form may be conditioned upon its participation in the mixture.

There are other, unacceptable views. **First**, the elements retain both their forms and the full unmixed intensity of their qualities, while the homogeneous intermediate quality is merely perceived owing to the extreme intermingling and the senses' inability to distinguish the parts. This is refuted by the certain fact that the elements do not retain their completely unmixed qualities when placed in contact.

**Second**, through their mingling and interaction all elemental forms are stripped away and none retains its special form. Instead they acquire one common form and become one matter with one form. Some make this new form intermediate between the opposed forms of the simples; others make it a new specific form of an actually existent species. Two objections are raised. (1) The corruption of forms, whether by attenuation or complete disappearance, must happen simultaneously or successively, both alternatives encountering the earlier difficulties about qualities. Qualities cannot now serve as agents in place of forms as they might be invoked in reducing the intensity of qualities: the destruction of the form destroys its effects, namely the qualities. (2) If the hypothesis were true, the mixed body would not yield different constituents through evaporation, distillation and calcination; but practical retort-and-alembic procedures show that it does.

First, the elements retain both their forms and the full unmixed intensity of their qualities, while the homogeneous intermediate quality is merely perceived owing to the extreme intermingling and the senses' inability to distinguish the parts. This is refuted by the certain fact that the elements do not retain their completely unmixed qualities when placed in contact.

Second, through their mingling and interaction all elemental forms are stripped away and none retains its special form. Instead they acquire one common form and become one matter with one form. Some make this new form intermediate between the opposed forms of the simples; others make it a new specific form of an actually existent species. Two objections are raised. (1) The corruption of forms, whether by attenuation or complete disappearance, must happen simultaneously or successively, both alternatives encountering the earlier difficulties about qualities. Qualities cannot now serve as agents in place of forms as they might be invoked in reducing the intensity of qualities: the destruction of the form destroys its effects, namely the qualities. (2) If the hypothesis were true, the mixed body would not yield different constituents through evaporation, distillation and calcination; but practical retort-and-alembic procedures show that it does.

title: True equilibrium and criticism of the Canon commentator
en:
**Authorial lemma: "Then temperament ..."** Having set out its nature and production, the text divides temperament according to *real* and *hypothetical* equilibrium, and according to departures from either by one or more qualities. Temperament was explained as an intermediate quality among heat, cold, moisture and dryness. These qualities are called "powers" because they originate changes, as appears from the physician's method; a power is a principle of change by one thing in another, insofar as that other is other. If the four powers are equal in degree and intensity, the temperament is genuinely balanced (*muʿtadil ḥaqīqī*); if not, it is unbalanced. Equality in the intensities of the powers does not require equality in the quantities of the elements, since one element may be small in amount but strong in quality, or conversely.

The author of the *Canon* emphasised equality by describing opposed qualities as equal in degree and *mutually matched*. The commentator on the *Canon* claimed that equality of their "quantities" refers to equality of the amounts of the elements themselves—just as two blacks being equal in *measure* means their subjects are equal in amount—and that their being matched concerns the equality of qualitative intensity. His reason is that he considers a genuinely balanced compound impossible: its elements would withdraw into their respective natural places before an enduring mixture could arise; equal tendencies would require equal bodily magnitudes and equal strengths of quality. He holds that what exceeds in quantity inevitably prevails in inclination, and qualities may help or hinder the specific form in producing inclination. Thus water chilled by snow is more inclined to its natural place than water heated by fire. A truly balanced temperament, impossible because of equal contrary inclinations, would therefore require equality of all elements in both quantity and quality.

He further argues that departures from such true equilibrium are not confined to eight kinds; no one, he claims, asserted this, since even hypothetical equilibrium and its eight departures form nine configurations outside the true one. This argument needs scrutiny. **First**, the natural meaning of the "measure" of a quality is its degree of intensity, not an extent or spatial magnitude that could measure the amount of the underlying element. **Second**, elemental qualities differ in intensity: fire's heat is reckoned many times the cold of water. How can equal quantities of the elements and equal intensities of their qualities be jointly imagined, such that impossibility follows from their tendencies to separate? **Third**, the eightfold enumeration of departures is explicit in the *Canon* immediately after its account of this very equilibrium. To object that hypothetical equilibrium and its eight deviations fall outside the true one rests on a confusion: all nine may themselves belong under one of the eight broad departures from true equilibrium.

title: A proposed objection to unavoidable separation
en: **Authorial lemma: "And that is denied."** The gathering of elements that leads to reciprocal action and being acted upon need not be produced by qualitative powers alone. title: Why no temperament is both hotter and colder than equilibrium
en: **Authorial lemma: "Or by two qualities that are not opposites; thus the kinds are eight."** One cannot depart from genuine equilibrium by simultaneously increasing both heat and cold, or both moisture and dryness. To move from the exact midpoint toward heat means that heat prevails over cold; it cannot at the same time mean that cold prevails over heat. This also refutes the proposal of departures involving three qualities, yielding four additional combinations such as hot-and-cold with wet or dry, and wet-and-dry with hot or cold. Such combinations could be imagined if equality of the magnitudes of the elemental bodies were also required for true equilibrium: both the hot and cold elements, or both the moist and dry elements, might then increase in amount. That, however, is a different criterion.

title: Medical or hypothetical equilibrium: species, kind, person, organ
en:
**Authorial lemma: "And one may call balanced ..."** What preceded concerned *real* equilibrium, from mutual balance in the sense of equality. The present sense is *hypothetical* or *medical* equilibrium, from justice in apportionment: a composite has received from the quantities and qualities of its elements the share appropriate to its nature and suited to its functions. Thus boldness and advance are attributed to the lion and fear and timidity to the hare; the former is suited by predominance of heat, the latter by predominance of cold. Medical equilibrium admits **eight considerations**. Suitability may concern the functions required of a species, a subgroup (*ṣinf*), an individual, or an organ. Each may be considered by comparison outward or inward: the species against other species, or against its own subgroups; the subgroup against others of the same species, or against its own individuals; the individual against others of the same subgroup, or across the changing states of that very individual; and the organ against the other organs of the same body, or in its own states.

For example, the human body, precisely as human, has a temperament more appropriate to it than that of any other species. If it changes or becomes corrupted beyond the relevant range, characteristic human functions are impaired. Yet its temperament admits a range between excess and deficiency; plainly not all human individuals have precisely one temperament, nor can every temperament support a human substantial form. Suppose, by way of illustration, that its heat cannot exceed twenty units or fall below ten, but varies between them. Above twenty the composite would not be human, but equine; below ten it would be a hare rather than a human. Between those extremes there is a midpoint more appropriate to the human as human than the temperament of any randomly chosen individual. This is the best human temperament and closest to real equilibrium. It would be found in an individual of the most balanced subgroup, at the age when growth has reached completion. Even though this is not the *true* equilibrium held to be impossible, it is exceedingly rare: physicians would treat such a person as a paradigm against which to measure others.

Similarly, the temperament most suited to a Turk *as a member of that subgroup* differs from those of other subgroups of humans. It has a breadth or permissible range: outside it the person would belong to another subgroup; its midpoint is most appropriate to that subgroup's individuals, though not necessarily best for the species as a whole. Likewise, Zayd has a temperament most suitable to him as this particular person, fitting his particular characteristics better than other persons' temperaments. It is that in which he ought to be if he is to be alive and healthy. Nevertheless it has a range, for his temperament in youth is not identical with that of childhood, middle age or old age. His range has extremes beyond which this person could not retain the relevant condition; its midpoint is that state in which his temperament is most effective for his functions, compared with his other periods of life.

So too the heart has a temperament more suited to it than those of the other organs. It has a range and two limits, beyond which it could not remain a heart, and a midpoint where it is as it most ought to be. Thus the total range of a species includes the ranges of its subgroups, the subgroup includes those of its individuals, and the individual's includes its temperaments in different conditions. The organ's temperament is not simply contained as another level in those ranges: they concern the whole body as *a whole*, in which warm organs balance cold ones and moist organs dry ones. The whole body's temperament cannot be identical with that of one organ.

It may be objected that an organ is itself a species of natural thing, with its own subgroups and individuals. Why not ascribe to it species-, subgroup- and individual-equilibria, each viewed inwardly and outwardly, instead of assigning the organ a separate parallel place? The answer is that this is correct in itself, but medicine considers both the human body and its organs as balanced or unbalanced. The body's temperament is assessed through the balancing of the temperaments of its organs: the heart's heat counterbalances the brain's coldness, and the bones' dryness the liver's moisture. When all the body's heat is compared with all its cold, and all its moisture with all its dryness, the resulting condition approaches equality and therefore true equilibrium.

There is, however, no actual intermingling, minuteness of divided parts, and physical contact between the parts of the organs in the temperament of the *whole body*, called individual temperament. It may be no more than their arrangement and relative disposition, or qualities that arise in the organs because of their mutual influence through proximity, without their parts being physically blended.
